Utilizing quantum mechanics and statistics, researchers have developed an intricate understanding of polymers over the years. However, the complexity of these models has hindered their practical application. The emergence of quantum Monte Carlo techniques has made it possible to accurately simulate long polymers, leading to the discovery of the "worm algorithm" which has since become the most effective method for simulating a broad spectrum of polymers. Nevertheless, the worm algorithm's reliance on time-ordered representations has limited its potential for studying chemically relevant properties of polymers. Our novel polymer inference method, based on the polynomial expansion of the partition function, allows for the representation of a polymer as a linear combination of its constituent monomers. This breakthrough enables us to solve the many-body problem of interacting polymers through an exact, non-perturbative calculation of the polymer's physical state using the worm algorithm. As a result, the combination of the polynomial expansion and the worm algorithm has facilitated highly accurate predictions of ring polymers' behavior when confined within cylindrical spaces. Our findings challenge the limitations of previous approximations, such as the saddle point and loop expansion, leading to the identification of new physical phases in confined ring polymers.

A single ventilator can effectively breathe for multiple patients if a suitable splitting device is employed, provided they have similar lung requirements. We've developed such a device in 3D-printable form, capable of ventilating two patients with different lung requirements using one ventilator. The device is composed of four 3D-printed junction pieces and four lengths of flexible tubing, all assembled simply. It utilizes the resistance to airflow within the system to regulate tidal volume for each patient, with accurate results verified through flow measurements with a calibrated flow meter.

Accurate automatic segmentation of the esophagus from volumetric medical images is hindered by limited and low-quality annotated data. This study explores whether pre-training deep dense attention networks on large, annotated CT datasets, such as liver-pancreas CTs, can enhance the performance of models trained on few low-quality esophagus CTs. We investigated two pre-training approaches: one using a Dense Unet with the attention mechanism and another using the Squeeze-and-Excaling (SE) block, evaluating their efficacy on low-quality CT data. Results from the Medical Metric Learning Challenge 2020 indicate that both models and pre-training strategies outperformed baseline methods and established a new state-of-the-art in the competition. Although the results are promising, further investigation with more comprehensive CT datasets is necessary to draw conclusive evidence that pre-training is universally beneficial.

Discovering oil reservoirs in real-time with a reliable evaluation process is a critical challenge. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) model, trained on a limited dataset, can be used to train an efficient evaluation algorithm known as Logistic-Maximum Likelihood (LMLL). The LMLLL method was applied to a reduced dataset with a technique called Likelihood-based Multi-layer Evaluation (LMEnRML), enabling a quick and efficient formation assessment. The results showed that LMEnRML achieved a 98.5% accuracy, outperforming a high-accuracy evaluation method (99.5%) while being 100 times faster. Furthermore, LMEnRML has the potential to provide a 1000 times speedup over real-time predictions. The LMEnRML method's unique approach with a multi-layer reduced maximum likelihood evaluation model offers significant advantages in terms of efficiency and performance. The study's findings also have broader applications, including the development of a novel algorithm called LMEnRML with multiple outputs.

Our research focuses on enhancing traditional named entity recognition methods by utilizing available context-rich information in text documents. To achieve this, we have developed a targeted approach called CER, which involves training a lightweight entity detection model through the selection of relevant subtasks from a larger text corpus. By carefully integrating external information such as word frequencies and entity types, our approach demonstrates significant improvements in entity detection rates, achieving a 5% increase in F-score on the OntoNotes dataset and a 5.5% improvement on the MSRA dataset when text-based decoders are employed.

We employ a specialized bitangent preservation technique in tropical geometry to rational curves, specifically in quartic curves, and relate it to the irrational bitangents found in algebraic geometry. By using this method, we aim to clarify the impact of tropicalization on rationality and identify conditions for irrational bitangents in the resulting tropical curves.

This research addresses a key issue: accurately estimating angles to nodes whose node IDs are unknown in a two-dimensional space. A novel algorithm leveraging Maximum Likelihood and grid search methods is designed to solve this problem. The algorithm's effectiveness was tested and the results show a significant improvement, especially near edges, with an average error angle of 3.15 degrees. These findings were verified and best performance was achieved with a 0.5 degrees minimum detection angle and estimated target location at (7.38 meters, 4.94 meters).

Multilingual societies around the world have identified critical needs for advanced natural language processing applications, such as education, governance, and knowledge dissemination, in their respective languages.  This has propelled the development of cutting-edge NLP technologies in a few prominent languages, yet a significant majority of the world's languages still lack access to these advancements.  To address this challenge, our research aims to introduce and advance NLP technology in low-resource languages, specifically in Dravidian languages, which encompass four major languages in South India and are widely spoken but have received limited attention in NLP research.  In this project, we outline our contributions to NLP in Dravidian languages, highlighting opportunities for meaningful impact in multiple domains, and discuss novel contributions made to the field, including open resources that facilitate future work in the region.  Additionally, we examine notable contributions made by our team and acknowledge areas for future exploration, such as phonology, computational linguistics, and NLP in Dravidian languages.  To facilitate the success of this research, we seek collaboration from the research community, industry partners, and funding agencies.

A significant number of individuals worldwide are affected by visual impairments, necessitating a shift in the approach to image descriptions. Currently, the method of providing picture descriptions through text messages lags behind the level of detail offered by the visual experience of seeing an image. Given the widespread popularity and practical applications of social media, which accounts for a substantial portion of internet usage, there is a pressing need to establish accurate image description standards. To bridge this gap, a new assessment metric named RevAUC has been introduced to evaluate the accuracy of image descriptions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this metric, a specialized neural network architecture incorporating contrastive learning has been proposed. This network, called DesContrast, is trained to generate precise image descriptions that convey meaningful information to other individuals viewing the same image. Moreover, DesContrast can be utilized to enhance the accessibility of images for visually impaired users by providing them with accurate image descriptions via text-to-speech technology.

This study explores the energy loss functions within TaO nanoparticles spanning 1-2 nm across three crystallographic orientations: cubic, orthorhombic, and monoclinic. By incorporating local field corrections, TaO's spin-orbit coupling is taken into account, which proves crucial for TaO's energy loss function computations in all three structural configurations. Our analysis demonstrates that local field corrections and spin-orbit coupling lead to the development of size-dependent plasmons in TaO, primarily driven by its lossy dielectric behavior in real space. To address TaO's challenge of obtaining experimental EELS data, our work offers a theoretical foundation for future TaO's energy loss function comparisons. Additionally, our findings highlight the disparity in energy loss functions among TaO's three structural variants, primarily resulting from the differences in their crystal symmetries.

Mishinformation poses significant threats to our political systems, social structures, and individual well-being. Investigating the online dissemination of false information requires a comprehensive understanding of its prevalence in our society. Surprisingly, little empirical research has explored the causes of widespread misinformation. We identify a key driver - a phenomenon known as 'The Big Sort' where individuals group with like-minded others based on geographical location. This specific sort amplifies the spread of misinformation due to location-based online interactions. To test this, we analyzed two large online communities in East and West Georgia, situated adjacent to each other. We found that online connections between these communities mirrored their physical geography, with local online interactions far outpacing cross-regional ones. Notably, we discovered that false political rumors spread more rapidly within these communities located in West Georgia compared to those in East Georgia. This difference can be attributed to West Georgia's more pronounced socio-economic segregation. Our findings highlight how 'The Big Sort' underpins widespread misinformation and emphasize the significance of studying local contexts in obtaining a broader understanding of our society.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have primarily centered on achieving superior performance in specific applications, despite the growing emphasis on developing versatile models. Such models, capable of functioning across diverse, unanticipated scenarios without the need for substantial computational resources or expensive data labeling, would have a significantly broader practical application. However, current machine learning and computer vision models, particularly deep neural networks, consistently require consistent training environments during both training and deployment phases. Despite the notable advancements made over the past decade, there is still limited research exploring the development of models that function based on non-stationary input data streams. Such models, according to the proposed paradigm, would be capable of performing accurate, unanticipated tasks using solely one-shot annotation, without the need for concurrent access to the original training data sources. The proposed approach, based on deep neural networks, utilizes non-stationary inference engines to transform unanticipated input data into features that mirror the characteristics of the training sources, thereby enabling improved model stability. Experimental results, as well as real-world applications, demonstrate the model's capacity to execute non-stationary tasks, including the use of non-Euclidean feature extractors enabled by the proposed method.

This study aims to analyze the consistency of semantic content in student speech while they instruct others to complete tasks. We focused on the influence of varying teaching methods, speech patterns, task steps, and errors on the core concepts in student speech. A dataset called CoRe (for consistency and robustness) was created to examine these variations. Using a BERT-based model, we assessed the semantic content in student speech and found that changes in demonstration styles significantly impacted the conveyed concepts. This effect was further amplified by differences in verbal expressions and errors, but could be mitigated by clear spoken instructions and accurate execution. Our results suggest that task errors can distort the speech used in teaching, but clear verbal expressions and correct task completion can counteract this tendency.

In our research, we developed an innovative algorithm for reconstructing ordered trees. The algorithm operates by determining the outdegrees from the bottom up, allowing for missing data as long as outdegrees are identifiable. The final stage involves verifying whether the reconstructed tree structure aligns with the original positive samples. The innovative aspect of our algorithm lies in its efficient use of linear time and space relative to the number of elements in the original tree, and it has interesting implications for decoding context-free languages.

A recent study revealed that finding the ground state of a quantum many-body system's Hamiltonian can be efficiently achieved through time evolution under the gradient flow of an appropriate functional, ultimately converging to the desired state. Building on this finding, we propose an alternative approach by substituting the gradient flow with a time-reversed unitary dynamics, which prevents system excitation and facilitates convergence to the target state. We formulate this new method via a specific optimization problem and identify its characteristic solution path as follows: a unitary transformation applied to the initial state that minimizes a combined measure of hamiltonian expectation and state norm at a given time. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness using two examples: a generic quantum field theory model and the flat space solution of the Euler-Arnold equations for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

Conversational systems are increasingly being deployed in real-world settings.
To ensure the reliability of these systems in various contexts, automated testing
protocols are being used. However, the complex nature of these systems and the
lack of standardization in testing methods have made it challenging to develop
a versatile and user-friendly testing tool. We have created a Python-based testing
framework for conversational systems that leverages the capabilities of concurrent
programming to facilitate the simultaneous execution of multiple test cases. By
leveraging concurrent programming, this tool enables the mimicry of persistent
user interactions while the system undergoes testing. It allows for a range of
outputs from the most basic to highly complex responses. The module is user-friendly
and straightforward to operate, and it can accommodate both immediate and
straightforward test scenarios. The tool has been successfully used to test the
conversational system known as AskUbuntu.

A previously unknown object with a mass comparable to Earth's could significantly distort the gravitational waves observed by LISA over long distances if it remains within certain limits set by solar system probes. Specifically, the object must not exceed a certain angular displacement in parallax and velocity relative to the solar system's barycenter. Under these conditions, its gravitational influence can be detected with high probability at a certain distance, or with even better detection chances at a greater distance. If the velocity and displacement remain within specified thresholds, it could be possible to locate the object using data from multiple observers, or even without doing so, or with very high probability within specific timeframes using existing or upcoming systems. Furthermore, both good and poor trajectories for the object's movement can result in significant distortions of gravitational waves observable by LISA within certain timeframes or distances. Additionally, in some cases, combining data from multiple systems can enable the detection of the object's transit across the sky with high accuracy.

This research explores the potential of a cross-lingual memory retriever to enhance the average case and challenging instances in automatic translation, building upon the Bilingual Memory Augmented Neural Translation model. By replacing the traditional BMM fixed lookup table with a dynamically generated, cross-lingual memory matrix, this model can access translation memories spanning multiple language pairs. The experiment results show that the cross-lingual memory model outperforms the BMM in both average and complex translation scenarios, even when the training data used for BMM is limited to the same language pair. Furthermore, a series of controlled tests demonstrate that the BMTS can successfully leverage training data from unrelated language pairs to enhance the translation quality for difficult instances.

The Planck satellite's data reveals the presence of "Hawking points" on the cosmic microwave background, potentially linked to the Big Bang's quantum gravitational effects. Theoretical models predict these effects would create a one-degree-sized, temperature-reduced circular area on the CMB. Our analysis of Planck's 2018 data confirms the existence of at least one such point, with a 95% confidence level, although its position depends on the choice of statistical test. Notably, the detected point aligns with a low-variance circle previously identified by Aghanim et al. (2018). Despite the findings' consistency with standard cosmological models, they challenge the cosmological principle due to the circle's distinct origin. The discovery's robustness may be enhanced by studying the circle's temperature, which standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology predicts to have a specific distribution. Our research indicates the detected circle exhibits lower temperatures than expected, which could be attributed to noise or the selection of a particularly unusual circle from the numerous circle patterns present in the data. Furthermore, we found the presence of Hawking points and low-variance circles is influenced by large-scale temperature fluctuations, which are in turn affected by $f_{\rm NL}$-type primordial non-Gaussianity, breaking the expected exponential distribution of the former and reducing the expected number of the former by up to 10 times. Finally, the detection of these features could provide a pathway to probing

This study applies the linearized flow technique to resolve a long-standing problem concerning the existence of time-periodic solutions for the Yamabe flow on a three-dimensional manifold without a boundary, where the scalar curvature matches a given negative constant. Specifically, this study addresses a previously unresolved issue related to a result by Wang and also employs global inverse function theory to solve problems related to Wang and Zhang as well as Wang and Wu.

In few-shot learning, a common challenge lies in the limited availability of training data, which often results in a lack of diversity and presence of normal task-related samples only. While current research has primarily focused on enhancing the diversity of task-related samples, it tends to neglect the elimination of outlier samples that can significantly impact the model's generalization ability. To overcome this limitation, we present a new framework for clean and diverse few-shot learning that simultaneously removes outlier samples and increases the diversity of the remaining data through a joint learning approach. This approach is made possible through the use of a query generator, which learns to produce different types of classification labels for each query, including clean task-related and outliery classification labels. These labels, along with the corresponding generated class prototypes, are then used to formulate auxiliary losses that jointly optimize the joint classification loss, the clean and diverse few-shot learning task. Our framework's effectiveness has been validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, which demonstrate notable improvements in model performance compared to existing methods.

In our work, we focus on the challenging task of recommendation when user preferences are explicitly expressed, often limited to brief descriptions or simple choices. To address this, we introduce Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE), a model that adapts to various input types and aspects. By incorporating an aspect-based preference encoder and an adaptive preference enhancement module, GAPE efficiently integrates user preferences into the recommendation process. Our approach achieves top-tier performance across multiple evaluation metrics and setups, as demonstrated in our competitive benchmark, with open-source code available for review.

This paper presents nature-based formulations for the minimum mean spanning subgraph problem, offering an alternative to traditional extended formulations. These new formulations utilize exotic cones in various forms to model selective sums of minimum mean spanning subgraphs. The research reveals that certain con formulations offer more compact representations compared to some extended formulations, even when accounting for graph symmetries. Specifically, the study derives both a 2^m-polytime approximation algorithm and a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the problem. Additionally, the research presents an exact algorithm combining selective sum solvers and outer approximation to solve medium-sized instances.

The composition of data used to train neural networks significantly influences the assessment of the data's ability to generalize to new MRI images. This problem is particularly prominent in the medical domain where data is often scarce. To address this issue, our proposed data evaluation framework evaluates data points independently, without the need for re-evaluating the model. It achieves this by training a small number of models with random subsets of labels and then using their predictions on unlabelled images to estimate a scoring function. This function is then used to rank unlabelled data points. We applied our method to a brain MRI image classification task and found that the model's performance on unseen images is highly sensitive to a common practice of using the same evaluation dataset for training. Our method provides a more reliable way to evaluate the quality of unlabelled MRI images.

We introduce a framework for network-based optimization problems involving multiple agents, where the setup allows each agent to define its own cost and constraints, and interacts with neighboring agents through shared variables specific to the links they share. This framework is designed to accommodate a wide range of optimization problems, including those that can be decomposed according to a graph structure, and we develop a method to solve these problems by applying the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers to the network's star graph representation, and we demonstrate its application to the network flow problem.

Researchers have investigated the potential of using Optane DC Persistent Memory Modules (PMMs) as server storage, which offers high performance for both random reads and small, uncompressed, persistent writes. To realize the full performance benefits, including during power outages, an optimized file system and persistent memory management system are necessary. We have developed NOVA, a novel relaxed file system for Optane DC PMMs, and evaluated its performance in various scenarios, for both correlated and uncorrelated write workloads. Our research demonstrates that for small, space-unconstrained writes, NOVA outperforms the default optfs in terms of throughput and latency reduction, achieving up to a 2.7x higher throughput and a 2.2x lower latency. Furthermore, replacing traditional spinning disks with Optane DC PMMs using optfs or NOVA, can decrease the latency of space-unconstrained writes by a factor of 4.2, resulting in a 2.2x higher overall performance for a popular database management system.

Andrzej Kieszewicz's motivation dynamics theory provides a mathematical framework for biological system design driven by feedback between physiological states and drive for specific behaviors. Building on this concept, we develop a multi-agent application that explores social behavior rendezvous in complex environments, particularly effective in understanding the interaction between people and their surroundings. Our framework's capabilities are demonstrated through its successful application in creating a safe and efficient meeting behavior for autonomous vehicles in an simulated urban setting.

Our study combines theoretical analysis and experimental data to shed light on the mechanisms governing the interplay between magnetism and lattice structure in the $x$Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ series of compounds. 111] direction using neutron diffraction for various samples with different Cm content (x = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20).  We observed a linear increase in the magnetic moment of Gd with rising Cm content, which was also reflected in the unit cell parameter.  On the other hand, the Rietveld refinement revealed a non-linear increase in the volume of the unit cell with increasing x.  To understand the given results, we used the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method to perform $x$Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ DFT simulations, which showed that the 4f electrons of Cm do not participate significantly in the bonding process.  As a result, the lattice expansion was primarily driven by the larger Gd and Cm atoms, whereas the exchange interaction was responsible for the reduction in the unit cell volume.

Quantum chromodynamics, or QCD, involves the interaction of heavy quarks like charm and bottom within bound states known as mesons and baryons. Calculating the behavior of these states relies heavily on lattice QCD methods, which utilize the Wilson-Coulomb gauge fixing to analyze the interaction between quarks. By decomposing the resulting color fields into potential functions, researchers can better understand the forces at play, including the tri-linear term in baryons and quark-antiquark pair creation, which play crucial roles in the formation of resonances. A detailed investigation of the potential landscape under this fixing reveals specific characteristics of mesonic and baryonic states, characterized by Susskind factors that influence the energy and spin of these particles.

Using the method of generalized descent right multiplication for the finite classical Coxeter group of type Bn, we rederive the exchange rules. We then apply this to obtain an explicit formula, through reduced expressions, for the generalized Green elements of type Bn.

A comprehensive set of 21 parameters defining the properties of galactic halos is assembled and analyzed, with 10 key parameters being constrained through a variance-based metric. Constraints are visualized using the $\Delta$-map method and a new set of dimensionless quantities that reflect the extremes in halo properties, both statistically and locally. This approach reveals that the most extreme halos exhibit distinct structural differences and that the mass distribution of star clusters in these halos spans over 15 orders of magnitude in mass. A combination of halo parameters is proposed to explain the observed range in emission lines of extreme halos. This analysis provides a foundation for refining cosmological simulations and enhancing our understanding of galactic halos' impact on observable phenomena.

This paper presents a novel approach to Houghton's equivalent relation and cyclic relation Houghton's relation by applying concepts from the functional Hilbert space theory, specifically utilizing the Dirichlet quotient space formed from the functions related to the five-dimensional stochastic equation related to the fluid dynamics of Navier-Stokes.

The primary obstacle in applying the silicon T centre spin defect to solid-state quantum technologies is the highly variable and confusing optical spectrum observed in groups of T centres. Although individual T centres may be excellent candidates for quantum applications due to their relatively simple and stable optical spectra, there is a lack of detailed information about their individual characteristics and how they interact with each other. To address this issue, we have employed time-resolved and high-magnification cathodoluminescence to study individual and groups of T centres in zirconia layers, and have been able to determine the root cause of the confusing spectral patterns. We attribute these patterns to optical spectral diffusion, which is driven by individual T centres interacting with nearby T centres in group spectra. By confirming that the T centre's nuclear spin provides protection against decoherence and enables long-lasting quantum memory, we have highlighted the importance of understanding and accounting for this spectral diffusion in future T centre-based quantum devices.

This paper proposes an innovative approach for tumor identification in medical images, combining Morphological Tools and the Region Growing Technique. Various detection methods were explored, but this specific method is focused on due to its effectiveness. Initially, the image undergoes enhancement to improve tumor visibility. Subsequently, morphological operations, including opening, closing, and gradient, are applied to eliminate minor objects and smooth the image, enhancing the accuracy of subsequent detection. The improved image is then subjected to thresholding to assign pixel values based on intensity, which helps in detecting the tumor. However, this may also detect other bright areas, so the Region Growing Technique is employed to identify and fill the tumor region by comparing pixel values to a specific criterion. Final detection is achieved by merging the outcomes of the thresholding and region growing methods, and evaluating patient age and symptoms to confirm the diagnosis. The method was implemented in Java, utilizing the Java Image Processing (JAI) library, and evaluated on a dataset of 50 diabetic foot images, resulting in a 98% accuracy rate.

In this study, we aim to extend the understanding of Bernoulli numbers to a more complex framework known as degenerate Bernoulli numbers. To achieve this, we first explore the degenerate Bernoulli numbers through various mathematical structures such as Circulant matrices, Galois fields, and Degenerate Umbral Calculus. Next, we establish a connection between the degenerate Bernoulli numbers and the classic Bernoulli numbers by leveraging Orthogonal polynomials. Finally, to illustrate our findings, we present computational examples using Mathematica.

The ultimate goal of using spectroscopic observations to monitor stellar activity is to minimize line list selection biases in reducing radial velocity (RV) noise. While previous studies have examined various line list choices, a deeper analysis of bias minimization had not been carried out due to the vast combination of line lists available. We have implemented a novel approach to randomly select line lists from the full set of available lines, a method that proves efficient in carrying out biased analyses on a large scale. We have applied this approach to analyze the Kepler-42 system using the HARPS instrument, comparing the results of a previous study with those from hundreds of line list realizations. We have investigated two line list selection strategies: a method based on selecting lines using a parameterized distribution, and a method that involves drawing lines without replacement from the full line list available. We found that the randomized selection method is significantly faster than the parametric one in reducing RV jitter and Doppler shifts, a result that was not predicted by existing theories. We also found that lines with intermediate equivalent widths are the most effective in reducing RV noise, contrary to what was initially expected based on the behavior of main sequence stars. The impact of line list choice on RV analysis is now empirically validated, and our findings suggest that analyzing multiple line lists and selecting line blends is the most effective approach for a bias-minimized RV time series.

This paper investigates designing low-power communication protocols for wireless sensor networks using hierarchical network sectoring known as Range Sectoring (RGS). 
First, we demonstrate how the RGS framework, where each node is assigned a range and sector based on its location within network regions, can significantly mitigate the prevalent hidden terminal problem while maintaining efficient inter-node communication in planar sensor networks. 
We outline a distributed algorithm for generating the RGS parameters that guarantees reduction of unnecessary message exchanges and achieves optimal results in reasonable time. 
The algorithm's complexity scales linearly with the number of nodes in each network region, resulting in small constant factors for the range and sector values. 
We also outline how Medium Access Control (MAC) adjustments can be implemented to minimize both communication and computation overheads. 
MacAddresses (MAs) are utilized to facilitate efficient data transmission and reduce computation in the lower-level network sections. 
Finally, we present the RGS-P protocol, which incorporates RGS and MacAddresses to create a highly suitable MAC solution for wireless sensor sections, specifically tailored to minimize computation and communication costs while effectively managing the hidden terminal problem.

The development of deep learning-based object detectors has rapidly advanced, offering excellent performance in a myriad of applications. However, selecting an appropriate detector for a specific context is not straightforward. In response, we propose a novel framework that facilitates the efficient evaluation of object detectors, taking into account critical factors such as input image resolution, classification accuracy, processing speed, and memory consumption. At the core of this framework is the object detector benchmark (ODB), a comprehensive database of over one million structured evaluations across more than forty detector models. By streamlining the process of querying relevant results based on customized criteria, users can readily compare relevant detectors for their specific needs. As demonstrated, the QDet interface built on top of ODB makes the retrieval of suitable detectors even more accessible. Furthermore, we extend the utility of ODB by formulating relevant querieies that lead to valuable insights, with the goal of guiding the future advancement of object detection technologies.

This note focuses on a specific aspect of a research paper by S. Daskalopoulos, J. Jost, and P. W. Yotsashilian, which examined the elliptic system described by the equation $D_{uu}u + \lambda (f_1(u), \dots, f_k(u)) = 0, u \in \mathbb{R}^k, \lambda > 0$. The condition for a solution's existence in this context requires the function $f_i$ to have a zero at an odd distance from the origin. We relax this requirement by allowing $f_i$ not to have a zero at any distance from the origin.

This study derives precise upper bounds on the expected values of functions of independent random variables that take on binary values, which are applicable to various concepts including entropy, score functions, and the Logarithmic Inverse function. Specific focus is placed on conditioning these random variables given their sum, though the findings can be adapted to other scenarios. Notable outcomes are achieved for convex functions, cubic functions, and general polynomial functions, which are derived and presented in the paper.

This article applies a concept introduced by Berthelot and Ogus, adapting the ideas behind it, to simplify some key equations from prior research. By leveraging this adaptation, the established connections between cohomology theories - specifically the relations connecting torsion crystalline cohomology and torsion étale cohomology through Witt vectors, along with the relations connecting torsion étale cohomology and Witt vectors via the Artin-Mazur trace formula - enable a streamlined proof of the relations showing that torsion étale cohomology and Witt vectors yield comparable results when considering absolute Frobenius on a finite field.

To measure the $X_P$-dependence of three-dimensional parton distribution functions (PDFs) in polarized protons through the single-spin asymmetry (NSU) in the process of inclusive D meson production, we propose an analysis of kinematically restricted, semi-inclusive (SNC) D meson production. The measure of the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in the interaction between the final-state D meson and its associated baryon number, when the parent quark is polarized, can be determined by applying Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics to pairs of non-flavored hadrons, selecting them with opposite or the same charge, in the process of inclusive or quasi-inclusive (QNC) D meson production. The quark level angular dependence is more directly reflected in the $\theta_R$ asymmetry in SNC meson production than in the twist-three quark asymmetry in inclusive (NSU) production, due to the presence of the parton level angle $2\theta_R$ in SNC, in contrast to the single $\theta_R$ in inclusive. Furthermore, the measurement of the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in NSU or QNC D meson production can provide a means to explore the di-hadron fragmentation function (DDFF) and hadron distribution function (HD

We develop the inverse de Sitter transformation, which is equivalent to the Fock transformation, and demonstrate that the De Sitter-invariant length measurement remains unchanged. The transformation can be expressed as a combination of Lorentz transformations and invariant length measurements within de Sitter spacetime. Additionally, we show that combining the inverse de Sitter transformation with a de Sitter gauge transformation yields the standard light-cone gauge formulation of the string within anti-de Sitter spacetime.

A system of invariants is described for the purpose of identifying conjugacy classes within a symplectic group $Sp(4,\mathbb{R})$. This description follows a set of established methods and references, which include Eisenträger and Sofronov's work on the $GL(3,\mathbb{R})$ and a related GL book. The invariants consist of a combination of a real number $\alpha\in \mathfrak a_{\mathbb R}$, a symplectic form $\beta\in \mathfrak p\cap \mathfrak p^{\theta}$, and a quartic polynomial $\gamma$ in four variables whose specific type is determined by $\alpha$. To facilitate the classification of conjugacy classes within $Sp(4,\mathbb{R})$, we adjust the possible values of $\alpha$, $\beta$, and modify $\mathfrak a_{\mathbb R}$ and $\mathfrak p$ accordingly. Additionally, an algorithm is established to uniquely identify each conjugacy class within $Sp(4,\mathbb{R})$ through the specified invariants.

This study introduces a groundbreaking entity representation framework, called
EREC, that seamlessly integrates topology and content to enhance recommendation
systems. By building upon the concept of Graph Neural Networks, EREC creates
innovative content-based nodes and sophisticated transformation pathways to
refine the traditional graph-based representations. Notably, EREC achieves
state-of-the-art performance in benchmark evaluations using three real-world
datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over existing graph neural network
models. The source code for EREC is publicly available on GitHub.

The end-stage kidney disease patient population experiences high mortality rates and significant suffering, with nearly two-thirds of the required number of available kidney donations falling short. The decision made by living kidney donors regarding the incompatibility level of their kidney in exchange donation programs is crucial to designing effective policies. However, the complex nature of the donor's decision-making process involves unknown elements, rendering the problem intractable using traditional matching program methods. This study pioneers the application of a Markov Decision Process model, treating incompatibility as an integral part of the donor's state, and discusses the implications of this approach before comparing it with the standard practice in matching programs. The discussion has far-reaching consequences for the understanding of the decision-making process in kidney donation programs, as well as the broader field of matching problems.

This paper delves into Bayesian parameter estimation of copula families using a comprehensive exploration of the Glazer Court case. Employing the R-INLA method, we examine three copula models: Frank, Clayton, and Gumbel-b, assessing their performance through both simulation and real-world application. The discussion extends to model comparison using conditional Bayes factors and the integration of Bayesian predictive densities for improved risk estimation. A key aspect covered is the estimation of joint extreme quantiles, a critical component in calculating Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for financial asset portfolios.

Financial documents serve as an important source of information, and the notion that "word usage predicts meaning" is frequently applied to extract semantic information from text. However, this approach overlooks the contextual role of words in conveying information. As a frequentist method, it also downplays the informational value of rare words and treats antonyms as synonymous with other words with the same usage pattern. Our research, which examines current embedding techniques on dental texts, reveals that antonyms are often conflated, particularly in texts with rare antonymous words. We also observe that rare antonymous words are not always equated with common synonymous words. Our findings suggest that contextualization, antonymy, and word rarity all play a role in conveying semantic information from texts. We argue that embedding techniques should account for the pragmatic information conveyed by rare and antonymous words.

This research focuses on enhancing waveforming fairness in broad bandwidth systems, specifically addressing fairness and efficiency objectives. By leveraging linear fractional transformation and convex optimization techniques, we developed methods to optimize fair and efficient waveform performance. The resulting algorithms, achieved through a low-complexity decomposition, allow for precise formulation and solution of fair and efficient performance goals in the context of waveform design.

Researchers have long studied Rayleigh-Benard instability in fluids, observing complex transitions from simple to chaotic movements as the Rayleigh number increases. Although numerous studies have explored this instability, many rely on overly simplified analyses, leaving a gap in understanding its full, naturally occurring dynamics. A significant challenge lies in the fact that the governing equations for this instability are highly nonlinear and cannot be adequately solved using conventional numerical methods, particularly when dealing with the massive data sets that result in the formation of convection rolls. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a physiological system that models the instability, enabling an investigation into its various states, including steady, oscillatory, and chaotic states, as the Rayleigh number increases across a wide spectrum. Through this analysis, we have uncovered novel features of the flow, such as a coexistence of multiple chaotic states that emerges at moderately high Rayleigh numbers. Furthermore, we have examined in detail a specific chaotic state that demonstrates sensitive dependence on initial conditions and an infinite number of periodic orbits, showcasing the splayed stable manifold of an unstable fixed point within regions where the flow is highly nonlinear.

Chomsky's observation that infinite languages possess ambiguous aspects has been a central concern in theoretical linguistics. This issue can also manifest in natural inference systems, where various proofs of the same statement may rely on entirely different underlying principles. This research presents a technique to derive ambiguous proofs of a target statement from infinite sets of potential proofs using a neural network-based method called Chomsky's Interpretation (COMI). The model employs a novel interpretation step to resolve ambiguities within the potential proofs of a target statement by assigning weights to the underlying principles employed in each proof. The comparative analysis of COMI's predictions and the principles of actual human-made proofs demonstrates that the model successfully captures the core aspects of natural inference.

This paper explores the concept of forming a prior through artificial rationality in the realm of multi-agent learning. It specifically addresses the challenge of learning to avoid repeatedly dominant actions within generic finite games. We propose a method where each player learns other agents' actions, including their learning algorithms, and successfully applies this in a multi-round learning scenario for the Battle of Sexes game.

To a large extent, our relationships with others are governed by our social networks, and these connections influence how behaviors spread, along with cultural norms, among people. A key aspect of network dynamics is rewiring, and in this study, we examine how both link formation and removal impact the progression of infections in a stochastic model. Specifically, we consider a dynamic process that mimics the Campbell algorithm, applying it to graphs where infection and health statuses vary, occurring on random regular trees. On these trees, where connections are continually established and broken, we determine the tree's expected structure and, consequently, the expected infection rate within the population. Notably, the algorithm's details dictate whether there is a fixed number of potential connections to consider, as seen in the Camp-Meidler algorithm. We aim to reveal how rewiring mechanisms influence the ultimate proportion of infected individuals within the population, as well as any associated fluctuations, and provide a detailed analysis of tree-based system behavior, including a comparison with the standard dynamic model where internal states are updated.

We examine a specific type of geometry, known as contact Sasakian geometry, in which a certain Reeb vector field possesses a distinctive property called a steady Cotton soliton. To understand this, we focus on a particular field, the Reeb vector field, within the context of a specific type of manifold, namely a (2s+1)-dimensional contact Sasakian manifold. According to research by Jiang and Zhang, this relationship can be described through a linear transformation, denoted as $\phi_X$, applied to another vector field, the Reeb vector field $\xi$, resulting in another Reeb vector field $\eta$. Additionally, we can identify specific examples of a geometry, known as warped product manifolds, in which the Reeb vector field exhibits a steady Cotton soliton property in certain types of contact Sasakian geometry, namely, a geometry formed by the combination of a nilpotent Lie group and a real line, denoted as $\mathbb{R}^l$, in a specific type of geometry, known as $\varepsilon$-Heisenberg type, in a specific type of geometry, known as $\varepsilon$-Heisenberg type.

When fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) to experimental data from diverse processes and at various $Q^2$ scales, the inclusion of DGLAP evolution ensures that the results remain consistent across different scales. This study undertakes an in-depth analysis of the CM15n LO (Leading Order) PDF set to investigate the implications of omitting DGLAP evolution in the context of next-leading order (NLO) and lower-order (LO) perturbative QCD calculations. As a result, we have developed a set of 'virtual evolution kernels' at both LO and NLO, which replicate the outcomes of DGLAP evolution but rely solely on the a LO PDF. These virtual evolution kernels have been examined in detail, particularly in relation to the longitudinal parton spectrum at the scale $Q=1$ GeV.

In this study, we introduce variance reduction-based experience replay (VRER), a novel technique for enhancing policy gradient estimators in reinforcement learning. By combining the long-term focus of policy gradients with the data efficiency of experience replay, VRER leverages a combination of historical and current data to reduce estimation variance. Our method achieves a favorable balance between the computational efficiency of policy gradients and the sample accuracy of model-based methods. Not only VRER provides significant gains in the stability and sample efficiency, but it also exhibits remarkable adaptability to a wide range of tasks across multiple standard reinforcement learning benchmarks, including the Mujoco, Anticlip, Hopper, HalfCheetah environments from the RLlib suite, as well as StarCraft II in the SMAC framework. To further support the community, we make our VRER implementation publicly available.

The recent release of Python 3 bindings for libcommute marks a significant milestone for the library, enabling users to take advantage of its highly optimized linear algebra functions while working with Python 3. These new bindings, known as cython bindings, have been developed in conjunction with C bindings for the library, offering users the ability to access libcommute's functions from both Python 3 and other programming languages. As a result of this cross-platform compatibility, developers can now easily share data structures and functions between these platforms, further expanding the library's capabilities.

Our study of the electronic structure in iron-based superconductors, specifically LaFeAsO, using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, provides key insights. Measurements of the superconducting gap at the zone corner are smaller than previously reported, indicating possible 'nodal' behavior at this location in '1111' iron-based superconductors. Near the zone boundary, the p-orbital gap exhibits notable splitting, resulting in an 's±' gap symmetry.

We have demonstrated that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization identity yield the same result, specifically by applying the transformation to the Grassmann-valued vector superfield within the context of the 2D Schwinger model in supergravity. Furthermore, we have identified a direct superbosonization identity corresponding to the fermionization of the complex scalar superfield within the first quantization framework.

Our analysis focuses on the angular distribution of lepton energies in the process of top quark pair annihilation into two jets and three leptons. By analyzing this distribution, we determine the spin asymmetry, which allows us to assess the top quark's polarization along the axis perpendicular to the top quark's motion. The measured asymmetry of -0.42 ± 0.09 (statistical) ± 0.09 (systematic) aligns with the Standard Model's predicted value of approximately -0.14. To refine the measurement, larger datasets from the LHC are necessary. The analysis exclusively leverages events with significant transverse momentum of charged leptons, helping to reduce background noise and improve the significance of the observed signal by up to four standard deviations.

The dielectric properties of LaNiO3 thin films, when integrated with SrTiO3, have been studied using microwave resonators and LaNiO3 thickness was varied to assess its impact on the fast-relaxing component's temperature dependence within the 300K to 20K temperature range. It's found that the LaNiO3 thickness significantly influences the component's two-level system-like characteristics, as evidenced by the distinct behaviors in samples with 3.5nm and 6.5nm LaNiO3 layers exhibiting linear and log-linear temperature dependencies of their relaxation times, respectively. The component's anormal behavior in samples with 4.5nm LaNiO3 layer, exhibiting the most temperature independence of its mean energy gap, was also investigated and found to correlate with the surface layer of the TiO2-terminated STO substrate, as confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The study's results suggest that optimizing the NiO3-terminated LaNiO3 surface layer may lead to a reduction in the component's discrepancy from the bulk material.

The main challenge in designing conversational agents that mimic human interaction is capturing the theory of mind, which underpins complex dialog tasks. We introduce a novel approach that utilizes neural architecture search to develop a unified, modular framework for solving multiple tasks within a conversational context. Our method automatically designs neural components that implicitly model the world and other individuals' knowledge, ensuring consistency across various tasks. We evaluate this theory-of-mind-centric framework on three distinct tasks: helpful Q&A, lies detection, and revenge. The results show that our NAS models consistently outperform hand-designed components in each task individually as well as across multiple tasks simultaneously, both in terms of performance metrics and theoretical understanding of the world and other individuals' states. Furthermore, our proposed framework is flexible, allowing designers to strike a balance between computational efficiency and performance, and easily incorporate pre-trained components for real-world applications.

This paper analyzes the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and phase shifts on the ergodic capacity of communications in reflective environments. We develop a method to evaluate this impact, which we apply to two typical scenarios. Our findings suggest that the ergodic capacity is largely unaffected by the correlation of the phase shifts and that its reduction is minimal in comparisons to independent phase shifts.

We introduce MG-GLAM, an accelerated C++ code in Python that utilizes OpenMP for parallelization, expanding on the existing N-body code GLAM. By leveraging OpenMP, MG-GLAM achieves a 2-4x performance increase over the sequential GLAM code while maintaining code simplicity. Through benchmark tests on various CPU configurations, we show that MG-GLAM matches the results of the original GLAM code and is suitable for reducing simulation times to less than a day, making it possible to perform production-quality simulations with reasonable compute resources. We also provide advice on selecting the appropriate MG-GLAM code version based on desired simulation speeds.

This research proposes a novel interpretation of complex, seemingly inert surfaces as inert representations of simpler underlying surfaces, akin to the relationship between the chordal SLE$_{8/3}$ and the real line, or the chordal SLÉ$_8$ and its imaginary counterpart. A key notion is introduced where the interaction between two boundary paths on an imaginary surface can be mapped to the interaction between multiple paths on the corresponding real line surface, utilizing the concept of conjugacy. As an additional benefit, this introduction of imaginary surfaces enables the calculation of specific statistical properties of boundary paths, such as their point contact distribution, no longer requiring the use of Schramm's fundamental factorization theorem, instead relying on the fundamental relationship between a path and its imaginary counterpart introduced by Le Doussal, Louvre, and Vasiu.

As an extension to InformedWiki, we introduce WorkingWiki, a wiki platform that integrates manuscript publication, user reputation evaluation, and software development. By combining these features, WorkingWiki offers a unified environment where authors can create and share research papers, peers can engage with the content, and developers can track and manage a project using GitHub. We showcase the capabilities of WorkingWiki using two examples: a CS manuscript and an CS project, highlighting its unique ability to connect academic publishing and software development through a reputation-based system that incentivizes high-quality contributions.

A statistical approach for modeling turbulent reacting flows has been developed,
based on applying a statistical operator directly to the closure equation for the
fluid velocity and temperature fields. Employing the eddy-damping quasi-linear
model and the thickened flame model, we compared various reaction zone models for
selecting appropriate averages. The post-selection analysis showed that the
progress variable flamelet model and the thickened flame model provide results
consistent with direct numerical simulation, leading to the conclusion that the
one-point probability distribution function is insufficient, necessitating the
consideration of higher-order probability characteristics.

We create an equation of state and thermodynamic relations for partially ionized gases with an ionization transition that isn't abrupt, which are then used to derive and solve the linear wave equations for different kinds of waves in one dimension. These solutions help us understand the behavior of different types of waves, particularly the ionization frequency and its effect on the acoustic and buoyant frequencies. The linear solutions for the ionization mode are compared to non-linear results from previous studies, as are the non-adiabatic limits for both adiabatic and non-adiabatic cases. Additionally, we model the behavior of partially ionized hydrogen gas and investigate the properties of the ionization region, which plays a crucial role in the global dynamics of stellar pulsations.

A new method for identifying synchronized clusters in dynamical systems has been
introduced, based on a novel link between synchronization and the rank of a
specific matrix associated with a given system. We have derived an analytical
expression for this matrix in the context of piecewise linear dynamical systems
and demonstrated its effectiveness through a study of the Ranken-Nullen
three-cell neural network. By examining this matrix's rank, we can determine the
number of synchronized clusters within the system and propose a method for
extracting their states. Our approach provides an alternative to previously
established synchronization detection methods and can be applied to higher
dimensional systems and those with more extensive synchronization structures.

We examine a one-dimensional spin chain composed of nearest-neighbor dimers on both generic and restricted lattice structures, specifically one where links point either left or right. In systems lacking inversion symmetry, particularly triangular and diamond lattices, we map out the complete phase diagram by analyzing the time evolution of a spin flip, revealing how dimers influence magnetization dynamics and identifying distinct time scales in triangular geometry. Conversely, we find that the broad parametric regime found in the square lattice persists in the diamond lattice. Using an exact time-dependent dimer concentration method, we uncover how lattice geometry affects dimer movement. Additionally, we extend our study to half-filled spin sites and non-interacting dimers using a giant impurity model, as well as restricted rectangular and trapezoid geometries.

We investigate the early universe's evolution with a specific scenario where extremely light dark matter interacts with conventional neutrinos in minute quantities. This subtle coupling has the potential to influence the success of the day following Judgment Day, also known as the Rocket Effect. We examine the implications of this scenario on radio astronomy observations, particle physics, and cosmology. The results of our research show that the effect of Rocket Risk is restricted to regions in the sky that coincide with the trajectory of a neutrino beam. Moreover, we find that research on radio astronomy can provide a unique insight into the properties of dark matter, specifically its mass and coupling strength to neutrinos. Furthermore, we show that this scenario is limited by existing experiments such as PS1904, KATRIN, and terrestrial two-neutrino double beta decay experiments. With no known obstacles in place, this model predicts a significant excess of neutrinos in the early universe, which could potentially be explained by a specific event in the universe's history.

Recent discussions on using ultra-high energy cosmic ray ensembles to investigate the distribution of magnetic sources require a deeper understanding of the spatial and angular properties of the ensemble members, particularly in the UHE range. We've employed the ray-tracing program Rairmpd to create proton ensemble projections based on photon maps from the EDEN model. The results show that the ensemble exhibits significant incoherence due to the scattering of UHE protons, with a characteristic incoherence length of around 1 Mpc. Rairmpd's analysis also estimates a source contribution of approximately 15% to the flux from the Blazar class. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this finding and the challenges associated with determining source contributions.

The recent observation of the gravitational wave event GW190425, which had a significant confidence level for its neutron star involvement, once again highlighted the need to examine the theory of nonlocal gravity. In this study, a new nonlocal gravity theory is scrutinized with the assumption that it is governed by a global variable in a metric-based framework. As the theory's nonlocal components only influence non-observable Christoffel symbols, it can be redefined to focus solely on measurable quantities. The revised nonlocal gravity theory is now consistent with the general relativity requirements for solar system tests and modifies the original theory's problem of singularity, effectively making it equivalent to a specific f(R) gravity theory in the case of vacuum. The original formulation of the theory's field equations is also clarified and investigated.

The burgeoning field of Programmable Conflicting Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) has yet to see a comprehensive design framework established. We present the first such framework, specifically tailored to the creation of simple, usable, and conflict-tolerant data structures. This structure enables systematic derivation of CRDTs by combining existing structures through well-defined operations. Our approach has been successfully applied to develop a range of novel data structures that handle conflicts seamlessly, including set, map, and hybrid structures, as well as complex nested structures with inherent time dimensions. Each newly created structure has been rigorously tested for its correctness, with over ten years of real-world usage on production systems, handling millions of daily operations, as evidenced by associated source codes and benchmarking tools made publicly available.

Understanding the connection between genetic variations and physical characteristics is a fundamental yet complex challenge. Although numerous methods have been developed to identify these connections through large genomic projects, a significant gap remains due to the lack of consideration for the structural nature of biological sequences, particularly protein sequences. While current approaches integrate sequence information for some types of data, they do not incorporate sequence information for protein sequences, which pose a unique challenge due to the high variability in their associations with physical structures. To address this issue, we propose using the association between protein mutations and physical properties to train deep learning models, which can then integrate this information to identify relevant genetic variations and their connection to physical characteristics. By conducting rigorous evaluations and comparative studies across multiple genomic variants and protein types, we found that incorporating mutation data improves the performance of models for certain types of traits. Furthermore, we found that the influence of mutation data varies across genetic locations and protein types, with the most significant variations occurring in certain types of traits.

Our analysis of the Galaxy's neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries reveals that their population is significantly larger than previously estimated due to an incomplete understanding of the galaxy's radio pulsar distribution. A revised model of the pulsar model accurately reflects their spatial arrangement and allows for a calculation of the galaxy's NSLMB population, utilizing a Beppo SAX/RCM spectral database. The results indicate a total NSLMB population of approximately 700, with the majority residing in the galactic bulge and disk, contributing negligibly to the NSLMB population associated with the galaxy's halo. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering the spectral properties of low-mass X-ray binaries in determining the galaxy's halo NSLMB population, which may be underrepresented in the Beppo SAX/RCM database. A Chandra spectral database is essential for obtaining a precise estimate of the galaxy's halo NSLMB population.

The measurement of one-dimensional velocity differences in single systems is often subject to large uncertainties. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method for calculating total velocities in binary star systems using their individual line velocities. This approach yields a significant reduction in measurement uncertainty by nearly a factor of three, achieving a precision of around 10 km/s for the total mass of binary stars spanning from 10^3 to 10^4 solar masses. As a highly precise and non-invasive technique, it holds great potential for studying the mass distribution in wide binary star systems. Notably, when observing the Orion Nebular Cluster, we found evidence of one-dimensional velocity concentrations exceeding the local standard of variance by more than one standard deviation in the range of 5-20 km/s among wide binary stars and their parent population. By applying our new method to velocity measurements in binary star systems, we may gain valuable insights into gravity's influence on these widely spaced stellar relationships. Additionally, the method's success could have broader applications to other types of wide stellar systems.

This study analyzed 34 sources within the low-frequency radio spectrum of the Perseus Cluster using data from the VLA FIELDS survey and the VLA HINTS survey. An examination of the spectral curvature in the range 0.5-15 GHz revealed a clear relationship with the sources' median fractional polarization, indicating linearly absorbed radio emissions. Additionally, a curvature/absorption connection was observed in the blazar subgroup. To investigate the correlation, a detailed analysis of the polarization angle distribution was conducted in the vicinity of dense absorbing clouds and the results support the absorption hypothesis. However, no such correlations were found near cloud centers with thicker or scattered sources showing multi-component structures. Estimates of absorbers' column densities and optical depths were obtained for the most prominent examples. A comparison with X-ray data supports the hypothesis of absorbed radio emissions lying in front of the sources' ionized counterparts. Finally, an investigation of the VLA FIELDS and VLA HINTS data revealed a potential overestimate of the absorption component's spectrum due to deconvolution convolution effects.

This study numeratically investigates how weak shocks in one-dimensional gas dynamics transform into strong shocks through interactions with planar impulses and expansions, focusing on the behavior of convex curves in related transformation mappings. By examining the characteristics of these curves' tangents and curvature, as well as the relationship between transformation end points, we derive a crucial relationship between shock transformation parameters. This leads to the identification of a stable strong shock solution resulting from specific initial conditions. Additionally, we apply a related transformation to analyze the relationship between tangent lines and transformation end points, providing a procedural approach to determine the properties of these transformation mappings.

Quantum interference resulting from the coupling of multiple core excitations to vibrational modes may significantly influence reaction barriers, potentially enabling more effective management of core excitation-vibration coupling to lower reaction barriers and enhance chemical selectivity. This study demonstrates the nearly simultaneous occurrence of quantum interference and a chemical reaction in a model featuring two coupled vibrational coordinates. The study shows that reaction dynamics are highly dependent on the relative phase between the core excitation and vibrational modes, and that quantum interference can be managed to minimize its inhibitory impact and enhance it to enhance reaction efficiency and selectivity. These effects are robust and hold true for a broad spectrum of model parameters. Moreover, the reaction's sensitivity to vibrational preexcitation can be leveraged to develop prepreconditioning strategies that optimize both yield and selectivity in accordance with available laser resources.

First, we provide a comprehensive overview of $\tau$-tilting theory, which emerged from the work of Auslander on almost split sequences, the contributions of tilting theory, and the development of $\tau$-tilting modules, which include a discussion of $\tau$-tilting finite modules, finite algebra, and special modules, and then present basic definitions and properties of $\tau$-tilting theory. Next, we explore applications of $\tau$-tilting theory to representation theory, including the development of $\tau$-tilting finite algebras, finite algebra, and special modules. Then, we examine Grothendieck groups, representation types, and Quiver with relations from a $\tau$-tilting perspective, and discuss the relationship between basic $\tau$-tilting modules and the combinatorial structure of Quiver with relations, as well as the connection between modules and Grothendieck groups, and the influence of relations on representation types. Finally, we discuss Gelfand-Ponomarev matrices and their connection to $\tau$-tilting modules, and provide a comprehensive overview of $\tau$-tilting theory, its applications, and the influence of relations on representation types.

In multi-turn dialogues, a common issue arises where the system's replies to a single user input lack variety, limiting the overall diversity of the dialogue. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach called Soft Contrastive Ranking is incorporated into a turn-by-turn conditional model for generating diverse dialogue responses. This approach selectively ranks conditions to broaden the range of sentence structures in the model's output, filtering out redundant information through a contrastive mechanism step by step. To validate the efficacy of this method, experiments conducted on the DailyDialog dataset reveal that the diversity of the model's output is significantly improved through the integration of Soft Contrastive Ranking. Furthermore, the approach achieves a balance between the coherence and fluency of the generated text, resulting in higher scores on both metrics compared to existing methods.

A new proposal for traffic scene action detection is developed in this research to enhance the reliability of next-generation driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles. Specifically, we focus on extracting action information from short video clips with embedded textual instructions, which are obtained from smartphones and other devices frequently used by drivers to seek help. To effectively process this information, we acknowledge the significance of action recognition but note the vulnerability of current methods to inaccurate instructions. In response, we introduce a action recognition framework that acquires the necessary information from traffic images and natural language instructions, designed to be robust against incorrect instructions. The proposed framework, which includes the attention-based instruction understanding module and the attention-based instruction fusion module, is intended to minimize the adverse effects of incorrect instructions on action recognition. The validity of our proposal was tested using a publicly available dataset called AssistanceAction, consisting of real-world driving scenarios where subjects requested assistance from action recognition devices. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposal in action recognition tasks.

Very small celestial bodies fail to generate sufficient core heat, maintaining 'cold cores' and potentially igniting a surface hydrogen fusion if angular momentum is high.  However, the impact of rotation on the critical curves for core heating remains unclear, necessitating an investigation into the effects of angular momentum on the curves, as well as the impact on the energy released from hydrogen burning.  Our research shows that the critical curves for non-spinning and rotating celestial bodies intersect twice in the HC burning curve, indicating a specific range of objects that can undergo core heating after surface fusion by burning their hydrogen.  In addition, the burning of hydrogen in rotating celestial bodies can significantly increase the internal heat generated, which has a notable effect on the critical curves and can lead to core heating in objects that would otherwise have 'cold cores'.  Furthermore, the critical curves for celestial bodies in rotation shift upwards due to the effects of a parameter that takes into account the impact of rotation on hydrostatic equilibrium, and objects near the boundary of cold cores and hot cores can be brought into the hot cores category by the introduction of spin, thus increasing the size of the population of very small celestial bodies with hot cores.  However, the effects of rapid rotation can also lead to a shift back into the cold cores category due to the limitations imposed on angular momentum.  As a result of surface heating in very small celestial bodies with high spin, the critical curves for hot cores move towards the direction of cold cores in the mass-radius diagram.

This paper explores the potential of using artificial neural networks for estimating densities, with a focus on a specific analysis involving hadron decays, specifically $D^0\to K^+-K^- -$. We employ a simplified model with a $C^2$ piecewise polynomial, Spline2, as a target for the neural network to learn. By applying this approach to simulated $D^0$ and $D^{*0}$ samples, we are able to accurately reconstruct the mass difference of a mass difference spectrum and the mass of a mass spectrum. The method also enables the precise determination of signal-to-background ratios in both spectra, and even recovers the lifetime of $D^0$ and the small width difference between $\pi^0$ and $D^{*0}$. Notably, we observe no significant bias in the reconstructed values of the mass difference, mass, signal-to-background ratios, and the $D^0$ lifetime plus width difference. The neural network's ability to model densities effectively makes it a valuable, flexible, and user-friendly tool in particle physics analyses.

A comprehensive subshock afterglow model has been developed to better account for the complex evolution of ultra-relativistic afterglows, considering the intricate interactions of shock waves with the surrounding medium. This model takes into consideration the various factors affecting the spectral energy distribution, including the ultraviolet instability, the dissipation of shock energy, and the generation of electromagnetic radiation. By doing so, it provides a more accurate representation of afterglow behavior over time, particularly during the transition between ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic regimes. The model's predictions can be used to analyze the observed light curves and spectral energy distributions of gamma-ray bursts, providing valuable insights into the physical processes occurring at the shock front.

We propose a novel approach to planarizing certain complex bipartite graphs by dividing their shared vertices, an application relevant to representing interaction networks among complex molecules like DNA polymers and proteins. Our method involves representing a complex graph as a series of interconnected, simpler bipartite graphs, and sharing vertices between adjacent subgraphs, and we demonstrate that this technique results in a planar representation, and derive a formula for the minimum number of shared vertices required for planarity.

A critical challenge in deploying deep learning models for image recognition is ensuring accurate score calibration especially in situations of class imbalance. Our comprehensive assessment of ten score calibration techniques reveals that these methods fail to consistently produce well-calibrated results in imbalanced scenarios. Moreover, our study reveals that the efficacy of scoring methods varies significantly across different tasks underscoring the absence of a universally optimal method. In addition to this finding we discovered that score transformation methods commonly touted as calibration techniques often result in worse outcomes compared to the baseline of employing output logits directly. Building on these insights we introduce two novel scores termed Transformed Margin Projections which exhibit exceptional and adaptable calibration capabilities particularly when adapted using label smoothing during training.

Bipeds rely heavily on continuous correction within a feedback loop to maintain stability throughout their movement cycles. This constant adjustment implies that any disruption to their control system, like the failure of their sensors, would have a lasting impact on their performance. To investigate this, we developed an open-source closed-loop walking controller for the Ghost bipeal robot and tested it with various types of data collection disruptions. Our findings showed that the effects of these disruptions on the robot's ability to navigate its path were temporary rather than indefinite. We established a relationship between the frequency of sensor data collection and the time it took for the disruptions to die out, as well as the magnitude of these disturbances. This relation proved to be a useful metric for assessing the robustness of the controller.

Our analysis reveals that when the underlying field is infinite, the first-order theory of the combined system is intertranslatable with that of the underlying field. Moreover, we demonstrate the ability to define maximal ideals within the ring of power series, even when the underlying field is finite.
