The complexity of spin-triplet superconductivity lies in managing Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interactions, whose influence varies by material. We present a novel method to precisely adjust these interactions through a magnetic exchange field in a non-centrosymmetric multilayer structure. In our proposed design, a spin-triplet superconducting layer is sandwiched between ferromagnetic layers lacking a center of symmetry. Calculations reveal that an applied magnetic field can induce a linear change in DM interactions, with the magnitude of this change determined by the materials' anisotropies. This method's versatility is highlighted by demonstrating its applicability across various material combinations.

The traditional assumption regarding the one-dimensional "effective" WIMP velocity distribution contradicts its one-dimensional counterpart and may impact the interpretation of direct detection experiments' results. To reconcile this discrepancy, we propose a method to identify the relevant effective velocity threshold based on the probability of measuring a specific 1-dimensional velocity, taking into account the full range of possible WIMP velocities within the local halo. This approach takes into consideration the relative likelihood of observing a particular 1-dimensional velocity, rather than simply the highest-velocity tail of the incident halo. For both the standard Maxwell-Boltzmann and drift models, we present calculated effective velocity thresholds along with the corresponding characteristic velocities, reduction factors, and expected global rates.

The effectiveness of individuals within public sector roles who depend on Google searches to acquire information can be hindered due to inherent prejudices in search results. Although Google's ranking system utilizes various features including the content of web pages and the connections between them, the influence of this latter aspect on outcomes is不明示. Although it is generally accepted that the connectivity between web pages affects search outcomes, the underlying mechanism driving this effect remains不明示. Leveraging the access granted by the Search Api to developers, we obtained profound insights into Google's connectivity-based effect on search results得到了阐明. The experiment conducted allowed us to form an不明示 model of the API's functionality, revealing the profound depth of its influence upon public sector professionals' information acquisition capabilities.

Consider a future high-energy muon collider capable of producing TeV-scale particles, for which we develop the random decay matrix in the SU(2) gauge theory using the Pauli matrices. With this framework in place, we propose several research ideas that take advantage of the special property of initial state particles - they have well-defined spins and can be configured in various ways, including aligning or opposing their alignments. By leveraging this unique feature, we suggest the following research possibilities: investigating Drell-Yan processes and triplet production of W bosons, studying top quark decays, in-penning of delta++ baryons, and Compton scattering processes.

To counteract pixelation artifacts in images produced by raster scan X-ray phosphor flat panel detectors (XFPPFDs), a novel sampling technique called rCASPR has been developed. Building upon the CASPR algorithm, rCASPR utilizes random sampling to increase image contrast and minimize reconstruction time, offering superior detail preservation and noise reduction compared to traditional linear sampling. Mathematical analysis shows that the rCASPR point-spread function exhibits optimal low-pass characteristics, effectively minimizing high-frequency information loss. Both theoretical and practical experiments confirm the effectiveness of this algorithm in enhancing XFPPFD image quality.

This paper introduces a novel concept called Control Barrier Functions with Implicit Constraints (ICBFs) and its extension ICBFs for higher-order systems. Our approach unifies and generalizes Control and Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, enabling utilization for a diverse range of systems - from first-order linear systems to nonlinear systems of any order. To handle ICBFs and ICBFs implications, we formulate iLearn, a novel algorithm based on Barrier Function Level Sets that efficiently manages safety-critical tasks for a wide spectrum of systems. As an application, we present the development and testing of an ICBF-based control strategy for ensuring collision avoidance in a higher-order quadrotor platform. The source code for the simulations and experiments is openly available at https://github.com/ashutoshgupta2000/ImplicitControlBarrierFunctions.

This study delves into the topological aspects of CF-approximation spaces, for which novel concepts, namely CF-closed sets and CF-convergence, are defined. Our findings establish a direct correlation between CF-closed sets in CF-approximation spaces and closed domains in continuous CQ-topological spaces. Additionally, we define CF-convergence to create a topological structure, the $\tau_{CF}$-topology, within the non-negative real numbers. The $\langle 0^+, 1^-\rangle$-open sets in CF-approximation spaces, along with their corresponding closed, continuous CQ-topological domains, and the $\langle 0^+, 1^-\rangle$-open, closed, continuous spaces, are examined. The findings demonstrate that every CF-closed set can be characterized by its CF-convergent points, and the topological structure, closed sets, and continuous spaces are fully determined within the framework of CF-approximation.

We have developed an advanced paired-permutation test that is 100% accurate, applicable to any dataset size, and  orders of magnitude faster than the typical Monte Carlo method used for large-scale comparisons in paired data.  In fact, even for moderately sized datasets (around 10^5 elements), the exact algorithm outperforms the Monte Carlo method by a factor of 10, making it unnecessary to resort to approximate methods in many paired data scenarios.

The global shipping market has historically been dominated by restrictive practices, including cartels that artificially inflated freight rates, ultimately leading to a significant drop in rates and increased shipping quantities their restrictions broke down in the early 2000s. To better understand this phenomenon, our model accounts for limited market entry, strategic behavior by firms in oligopolistic markets, and varying cartel participation levels, providing policymakers with crucial price predictions to evaluate specific policy interventions. Notably, our findings suggest that significant reductions in barriers to market entry and anti-trust measures may not be enough to replicate the substantial decreases in rates observed following the collapse of cartels, highlighting the need for more aggressive measures to promote market competition.

We have previously proven the existence of a method for converting any loom space into a geometric triangulation that resides within a Banach space. In this work, we explore the conditions under which this method can be streamlined into a piece-linear triangulation embedded in a Euclidean space.

Deep learning models, particularly those tailored for node classification, have gained significant popularity in recent years due to their ability to integrate both label and structure data. While the models' accuracy heavily relies on node attributes, the graph's inherent connections often play a more pivotal role in achieving high performance compared to node attributes alone. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a thorough investigation by analyzing the contribution of graph structure to model performance, yielding several key insights that previous studies had overlooked. Our research reveals that different neural network components process and utilize graph connections in varying ways, with certain components being particularly responsible for leveraging the model's ability to classify nodes accurately. A comprehensive assessment was performed by separately evaluating both the graph connections and node attributes' impact on performance, resulting in measurable quantifications of their respective contributions. To further validate our findings, we experimented with node classification models applied to diverse networks and achieved consistent outcomes across all cases. Our research yields novel insights that can guide the development of future graph neural network algorithms by identifying parts of these models responsible for leveraging node attributes and graph connections respectively. Our findings indicate that certain components of graph neural network models rely heavily on graph connections, with little consideration given to node attributes, while other components effectively combine node attributes to produce a beneficial effect. Our research was conducted by analyzing the node classification model's performance in a thorough ablation study, yielding quantifiable measures of graph connections and node attributes' impact on performance across diverse network types. A contemporary estimator-based dimensionality reduction technique IAR(g) is introduced which determines optimal parameters adaptively to achieve a balance between bias and variance in traditional estimators' power function adjustment. The proposed method demonstrates superior robustness to data contamination compared to the jazz band estimator's input adjustment, exhibiting stable performance across various contamination levels and types with minimal average increases in mean squared error of 1.5%. The researchers also explore the application of iterative dimensionality contamination handling (IA^2) which addresses both data contamination and chosen 'good' gene expression profile simultaneously through multiple rounds of PCA iterations until convergence. The superiority of IA^2 in maintaining biologically relevant results even with high levels of data contamination and multiple rounds of iterations is demonstrated through experiments on microarray breast cancer data.

Recent works by Sanders, G. and Wong, T. provide a comprehensive framework for analyzing the geometries of singular area minimizers at a technical level. Building on this analytical style, the book expands the original concepts in technical detail and offers a wide range of examples across various fields of mathematics, including the classical proof of the Poincaré conjecture in dimension three, Pu's theorem, the Pohozaev identity, and the Pansu asymptotic geometry of singular metrics with conical singularities.

In superconductors, the presence of a moving magnetic flux line or vortex creates an entropy within its core due to the coexistence of normal and superconducting states, in contrast to the low entropy found outside the core where only the superconducting state exists. This phenomenon leads to the emission of thermalized phonons from the vortex, resulting in localized heating and a reduced temperature gradient in its immediate vicinity. In theory, the vortex acts as a moving source of heat, in contrast to conventional thermoelectric devices that transfer cold. We propose that vortices could be utilized to drive the refrigeration cycle in microelectronic devices by driving the vortex through the application of an electric current, and that vortices may also have a higher entropy, and thus a larger Seebeck coefficient, compared to the charge carriers that drive the vortex. Furthermore, we show that in type II superconductors, where vortices are quasi-one-dimensional objects, the entropy within their core far exceeds the entropy associated with the charge carriers that drive them.

This paper proposes a novel, decentralized approach for efficient communication and cooperative adjustment of distributed system loads. The method, based on maximum entropy feedback (MEF) theory, allows for a single-bit message to be transmitted from the aggregator to the distribution network, conveying essential system information. By leveraging MEF, the approach ensures that the load adjustment process remains statistically uncorrelated with the current system state, facilitating effective operation even in the presence of limited data transmission. The method's viability is demonstrated through the development of a virtual power plant, where a unique optimization algorithm enables the conversion of a singular message into a system-wide indicator. The results presented in the study show that maximum entropy feedback can effectively facilitate communication and load management in complex power distribution networks. The approach's performance and uniqueness are verified through numerical experiments, which demonstrate its ability to achieve near-optimal load control and communication performance.

This research addresses the challenges and ethical issues associated with creating machine learning models that can forecast financial markets, specifically focusing on Fintech. We developed a cutting-edge machine learning model for stock prediction by integrating technical analysis and moral considerations into traditional predictive modeling. Our approach leverages advanced machine learning algorithms, namely XGBoost and LightGBM, to analyze patterns in technical indicators and price histories. We enhanced these models' performance by optimizing hyperparameters and addressing class imbalances. Our experiments, conducted on real-world stock data, showed that our enhanced models outperformed traditional methods, with improvements up to 15% in key evaluation metrics. We open-sourced our code and models to facilitate future research in this field.

The event GW190425B, a potential binary white dwarf merger resulting in a supernova event, is the focus of our research. By combining observations of the associated supernova event, BT2019gj, with the parameters of GW190425, we found a significant discrepancy. Specifically, the estimated mass of the progeny from the merger was 2.8 solar masses, exceeding the typical explosive supernova masses of 1.4-1.5 solar masses. Moreover, the supernova characteristics of BT2019gj did not align with those of a standard thermonuclear supernova. In light of this mismatch, we hypothesize that GW190425B may represent an unusual type of thermonuclear supernova event, arising from the fusion of two white dwarf stars.

A reorganization of the EFT framework is proposed to facilitate a more direct interpretation of its theoretical and experimental implications. As an illustration, the approach is applied to the study of the trilinear Higgs boson coupling within the context of DHC and DHCM scenarios. The LHC's ability to constrain the Higgs self-coupling through the analysis of double Higgs boson events is central to this discussion. The relationship between the five-dimensional spacetime parameter in a model and the corresponding effective field theory is examined. Furthermore, the LHC's capability to place limits on four-Higgs boson scattering processes is explored. The connection between the leading-order five-Higgs boson scattering cross-section in effective field theory and its counterpart in four-dimensional spacetime is analyzed. The proposal suggests utilizing a hybrid framework that combines four-dimensional effective field theory with a set of well-defined physical parameters inherent to fundamental theories, including Higgs self-couplings, to enhance the interpretability of LHC experimental findings.

In our study of the pre-non-relativistic parametrization in general relativity theory, we found that setting the spatial components of the metric to zero enables an analytical and systematic $c^{-1}$-power series expansion. This series can be easily organized due to the metric's dependence on $c^{-1}$ only appearing in the determinant term. Additionally, this method offers the advantage of providing an analytical and consistent approach that does not rely on the $c=0$ initial condition, which often leads to divergent series. This 'pre-relativistic' state serves as an intermediate and convenient starting point for completing an analytical generalization of the Newtonian limit. To demonstrate the practical application of this method, we applied it to two initial metric models, obtaining consistent series expansions up to the post-Newtonian order 5. Our approach can be extended to other analytical gravity models, as the condition of vanishing spatial components of the metric is not exclusive to GR.

We revisit the holographic computation of scalar field expectation values and decoupling techniques, given the issues with naive calculations at small radii in AdS$_3$, as discussed in [1, 2]. Our method for AdS$_3$ involves reformulating the Einstein equations for the boundary metric as a set of two separate differential equations, rather than one. This leads to a critical finding that only the 'source' mode of a scalar field contributes to the holographic computation of the radiative energy-momentum tensor, a result that contradicts earlier assertions made in literature, as shown in examples such as global AdS$_3$ with a scalar field in sections three and four. Moreover, our approach allows us to explicitly demonstrate the equivalence between our method and the 'decoupling method', as well as the 'geometric decoupling method', as per [1]. In a broader context, given the limitations of the classical approximation in predicting small-scale behavior of quantum sources, as per the Faulkner-Wittkowski-Zaanen work, we hypothesize in section five that the 'source mode only effect' may have a quantum counterpart.

We investigated how a long intruder, in a shape of a cylinder, moving perpendicular to its axis affects the surrounding granular material. This study took place in both gently sloped and vertically positioned channels, with the channel's width being comparable to the intruder's diameter. High-speed cameras recorded the intruder's motion at various speeds, resulting in data on the drag forces exerted on it. We used a fast intruder to stimulate the intruder to follow the channel's curvature, thereby measuring the drag forces acting parallel to and perpendicular to the intruder's length. We found that in all experiments, the induced flow was confined within a wedge-shaped region, with an angle of approximately 26.5 degrees, and that the intruder's speed had a significant impact on the drag it experienced. Specifically, we observed that the drag increased linearly with the intruder's speed, with an onset speed of approximately 0.29 meters per second, below which the drag was found to be constant and equal to the drag experienced when the intruder was stationary. We also found that the angle of the wedge and the constant drag were unaffected by changes in the intruder's density, diameter, or surface properties, as well as the angle of the inclined plane, within certain ranges. We used these findings to develop a theoretical model that could explain the observed behavior, including the angle of the wedge and the increase in drag at lower intruder speeds, in terms of power-law equations.

Observations of intense star-forming disk galaxies show that powerful ionised gas outflows have a significant impact on them. By leveraging optical spectroscopy from the VLT in highly intense star-forming galaxies at a redshift of 1.7, we detected optical emission lines from these galaxies. Our findings demonstrate that a substantial amount of kinetic energy is being transferred to the ionised gas by these outflows, which is nearly equal to the total radiative energy from both ionising photons and massive stars. These outflows have a gas depletion timescale that is shorter than the timescale required to consume all the gas through star formation alone, which suggests that mass outflows from these galaxies have a significant effect on their evolution at an early stage. Our results also indicate that the ionised gas and molecular gas have similar outflow speeds, which is surprising given the difference in mass between the two types of gas. This indicates that optical lines can be used to study molecular gas outflows.

Finding the optimal configuration for a system is a recurring and vital task.
Traditionally, experts rely on experimentation, simulation, and testing to identify configurations that yield the best results. In contrast, automated methods using reinforcement learning can efficiently discover configurations by training multiple instances of a system in parallel and leveraging shared knowledge to guide the search for the best configuration. However, this approach becomes resource-intensive when applied to complex systems with numerous parameters. To address this challenge, we introduce BoAnon, an advanced architecture based on the multi-agent anonymous communication learning framework, where individual agents specialize in exploring specific regions of the configuration space, but can still benefit from the collective knowledge of the group. By employing the anonymous communication framework, agents can exchange configuration-value data without revealing their identities, thereby protecting the integrity of the system from potential threats. Our extensive evaluation on benchmark scheduling problems demonstrates that BoAnon can significantly outperform a non-anonymous baseline and achieve efficient configurations with high performance results.

Our analysis of 20% most central Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV reveals the connection between triangular flow and particle density gradients near midrapidity in small systems. By examining the relationship between average transverse momentum and nuclear collision centrality for various particles in these small systems, we found a pattern nearly identical to that observed in larger systems, supporting the universality of transverse thermodynamics across different particle types. Moreover, adding elliptic flow to the picture confirms small systems produce hotter particles and larger fluid velocities, consistent with findings from earlier experiments.

Our research team at University of Warsaw and CNRS-LIRMM, along with our partners, is tackling the challenge of semantically annotating vast datasets consisting of over a billion interconnected data points. To address this issue, we've developed a novel quality measurement指标 called DecoQualityAssurance, which can efficiently gauge the trustworthiness of these datasets without requiring time-consuming, query-based calculations. Specifically, DecoQualityAssurance leverages a representative, randomly selected subset of these datasets to accurately predict their overall integrity. We've also presented an innovative algorithm that swiftly executes the necessary calculations using advanced graph processing techniques on both traditional computers and distributed systems. The findings from our comprehensive experimental analysis demonstrate the method's remarkable speed and precise results when applied to real-world datasets of different sizes.

We develop uniform large sample theory for independent increment and process density models estimated using minimum density power divergence methods. Our results, applicable in probability and $L_2$ norms, provide insights into the asymptotic behavior of these estimators and confirm their consistency with maximum likelihood estimation as the skewness parameter $\kappa$ increases. Our framework also accommodates a broader range of functions than the identity link function used in log-linear modeling. Furthermore, our study extends to independent processes and provides an alternative proof for the consistency of independent regression models estimated using MDPD.

The observable properties of gas within active galaxies are significantly altered by shock-ionization processes, affecting line ratios and emission velocities to varying degrees. A unified model has been developed to model the diverse line profiles observed in the spectra of active galaxies through the combination of a line profile from the broad line region and an additive Gaussian component attributed to ionized gas. This additional component is influenced by the strength of the gas component relative to the broad line region, as depicted by the ionization parameter. Notably, the model predicts that the Gaussian component becomes more apparent in galaxies with stronger broad line components, typically associated with a type Ia relationship, while in type Ib and c AGN, the greater asymmetry in the broad line region line profile may mask the additive Gaussian component. Furthermore, the model is capable of explaining the characteristics of the ionized component in some narrow line magnum narrow line galaxies through the interaction between a highly relativistic jet and the broad line region, while activating a nuclear shock that leads to the activation of the nucleus.

IoT applications are increasingly common, but they often suffer from security issues due to their complex and interdependent nature, which makes them difficult to test. To address this challenge, IoT applications require a framework that facilitates their efficient testing. To respond to this need, the Frisbee framework was developed to facilitate the testing of IoT applications. The Frisbee framework offers a comprehensive set of capabilities, including the ability to create component and system specifications, to model system behavior, and to verify the correctness of the system with respect to its specifications. The Frisbee framework has been shown to effectively test the IoT application in a modular and targeted manner, and the testing process can be streamlined and automated. The Frisbee framework has been demonstrated to effectively test the IoT application, and the process can be streamlined and automated. The Frisbee framework has been shown to effectively test the IoT application, and the results indicate a significant improvement in testing efficiency and precision.

Recent discoveries at the Large Hadron Collider by the LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS experiments have relied heavily on precision physics, which the LHCb experiment excels at. The LHCb experiment, located in the LHC tunnel, is uniquely positioned to study rare decays of B mesons, such as the decay of a B_s meson into a muon-antimuon pair, as well as leptonic and semi-leptonic decays of B mesons, which offer insight into the masses of heavy quarks, such the bottom and charm quarks. Furthermore, these precision measurements, along with CPLEAR and DUNE neutrino experiments at the LHC, can provide a deeper understanding of the lepton flavour universality and the difference between matter and antimatter, respectively. We discuss the capabilities of the LHCb experiment in these areas, highlighting the critical nature of the flavour and CP universality tests, the determination of heavy quark masses, and the neutrino experiments, which the LHCb experiment, the LHCb experiment, and the LHCb experiment can contribute to.

A neural network-driven traffic scene generation model is a crucial component in crafting high-quality data for self-driving vehicles. Although several approaches have been developed, many of them suffer from limited diversity due to their autoregressive nature. To address this challenge, we developed SceneGap, a model that incorporates an occlusion module and treats visible sensor data as ground truth. By iteratively refining its predictions through comparison with real data, SceneGap overcomes the constraints of traditional autoregressive models. Unlike other non-mariative models that prioritize efficiency, SceneGap achieves a balance between accuracy and diversity. Its performance is further enhanced by incorporating transfer learning. When pitted against state-of-the-art methods, our model demonstrated significant improvements in traffic scene modeling. Moreover, SceneGap demonstrated its capability to produce high-quality training data for object detection models.

A key feature of the Ising model on a Cayley tree is its alignment with a group representation, which facilitates precise computation of the partition function via a transfer matrix. Leveraging this, we apply the Ising model to an underlying representation group of a Thorngren-Zelevinsky group, which has been utilized in computing character degrees and has numerous subgroups with rich theoretical importance. By determining the partition function's transfer matrix on this representation, we contribute to the study of the phase transitions on the resulting tree, which has been thoroughly analyzed.

This article presents an innovative variant of the standard FGMRES iteration, referred to as the real-valued complex FGMRES (RCFGMRES) method. The RCFGMRES subspaces, built through the application of a specific transformation matrix to a traditional FGMRES subspace, numerically demonstrate the capability to solve real-valued systems even when employing complex arithmetic. The RCFGMRES algorithm's effectiveness is illustrated through both numerical experiments and theoretical support, which include a data rank-based termination argument. The numerical results and examples clearly demonstrate the utility of RCFGMRES, with implementation instructions provided for a FGMRES solver within the scipy package.

This research paper focuses on complex dynamical systems that evolve in discrete time within a two-dimensional space. We have established several key results in this area, including resolving two prominent unanswered questions. The discoveries made here are meaningful as they carry implications beyond the immediate context, particularly in relation to long-standing issues in arithmetic combinatorics and stochastic processes. Specifically, we have obtained key insights regarding the recurrence of patterns in systems that mix rapidly, systems exhibiting wandering behavior, and understanding synchronization, coordinate changes, and factor maps. To achieve these insights, we developed a novel mathematical framework that combines return time analysis with a constructed set of options, alongside a new method for examining systems through time-discrete mapping.

We examine the evolution of superbubbles (Sups) created by massive star clusters in galaxy disks, focusing on dust formation and destruction within these environments. By integrating a detailed dust model with established Supb evolution and stellar population models, the dust composition is tracked from its birth through various processes to its final fate. The dust formation rates, both from core-collapse and pair-instability supernovae, are crucial factors influencing the overall dust budget of Sups. The effects of pair-instability supernovae are especially significant in environments hosting very massive stars greater than 100 solar masses. Dust formation by pair-instability supernovae is likely the dominant process in such environments. The dust formed is initially located in the disk, but is eventually ejected into the galaxy's halo for the most massive clusters. The core-collapse supernovae and photoelectric heating of the Supb's interior also have a substantial impact on the overall dust distribution. The former increases dust formation rates in core-collapse supernovae, while the latter causes dust destruction within the Supb's cavity. The dust that escapes the Supb and joins the surrounding gas is generally located for the most part within the disk, as pair-instability supernovae are associated with core-collapse in these environments. The dust escape fractions are 0.1-10% for core-collapse and 10^-4-10^-2 for pair-instability, with the Supb dynamics and dust formation/destroy rates influencing the dust escape

This research addresses the challenge of identifying 3D objects at long distances using image sensors by combining the strengths of color image and lidar data. We present a novel approach that leverages both RGB and lidar information to enhance the detection of objects in distant ranges. By employing the RGB detection method to supplement the lidar data, we aim to provide a robust solution to this problem. Our model uses the RGB detection result to inform the lidar detector, with the intention of improving the overall detection performance. We propose a specific implementation of this framework where the RGB detection result is used to influence the lidar detector through an additive modification to the lidar feature map. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in the face of limited computing resources. Moreover, we present the first public dataset consisting of real-world far-field 3D object detection annotation data. The data set contains 150,000 images with object bounding box annotations, categorized into ten different types of objects. The data set is used to evaluate the proposed detection method and other approaches to 3D object identification. Our experimental results show the superiority of our model over the baseline method, with an overall detection mean average intersection over union (mIOU) score of 34.1%, a 2.1% improvement over the baseline model.

A primary objective of computational chemistry and quantum chemistry is to accurately model electronic structures and calculate potential energy surfaces. Using large-scale electronic structure methods as targets, we've developed a quantum machine learning approach using ansatz generators to efficiently prepare quantum states on the potential energy surface. As an application, we used a smaller VMC test set to demonstrate the model's ability to accurately fit multiple FCI targets within energy eigenstates of $10^{-3}$ Hartree, achieving a lower energy variance than traditional multireference methods. Furthermore, an adaptive learning method was utilized to find the ground state of liquid water dimer via diffusion Monte Carlo with an energy as low as -24.21 mEh and a significantly reduced variance.

During heart surgery, registering a 3D model of the heart to real-time, noisy data is complicated by the organ's irregular and unpredictable movement. The success of this process is crucial, as it directly impacts the accuracy of subsequent analyses. We propose an approach that achieves robust registration of the heart model to motion-captured, point-cloud data obtained from electro-anatomical mapping systems. Our method employs a previously developed, complex heart model that incorporates prior knowledge, multi-scale organ tracking, and data scaling. The key component of this approach is a likelihood function designed to accurately match the model's surface to the scattered sensor data points, accounting for scattered noise. The suggested method was tested and showed positive results, indicating its effectiveness in registering the heart model to the mapping data. The code for this approach is publicly available.

The relationship between a matter collineation and its associated conservation laws can be non-existent, as demonstrated by the fact that the conformal condition may hold even when the energy-momentum tensor has limited degrees of freedom. In such cases, researchers have found alternative criteria based on a degenerate conformal curvature tensor and identified their corresponding collineations. Furthermore, a detailed examination of flat spacetime and specific matter distributions has revealed examples of degenerate conformal matter collineations with associated collinear conformal curvature tensors.

Self-supervised methods for flow estimation have progressed significantly, particularly in achieving high accuracy in texture-rich objects. However, dealing with highly occupied regions, such as when objects block the view of other surfaces, remains a challenge in most methods. Although occlusion handling techniques exist, many of them are complex and require post-processing to generate overestimated flows, delaying the method's training speed. In this paper, we present a self-supervised method for flow measurement that focuses on accurately modeling the flow of both moving and stationary objects within the context of flow fields, without needing depth information. By directly modeling flows in both frames and introducing new loss functions for identifying flow ambiguity and optimizing the overall model. The proposed method achieves high accuracy in benchmark datasets and outperforms other methods in the KITTI dataset when evaluation criteria are the same, demonstrating superior efficiency and speed of at least five times in comparison.

This study introduces a novel neural network architecture, the Adiabatic Neural Network (ANN), which serves as both a high-performance and versatile classification tool, rivaling conventional ANNs in efficiency but with significantly reduced power consumption. The proposed network's design leverages the特性 of phase transition in materials to utilize inherent memory, effectively eliminating the need for excessive flip-flops for data storage. Furthermore, the Adiabatic Neural Network can memorize input information within its intrinsic cellular structure, enabling it to function as a self-contained data pipeline for training deep learning models. The adiabatic circuit's inherent sensitivity to initial conditions allows the Adiabatic Neural Network to perform stochastic gradient descent, a key algorithm for training deep learning models. Numerical simulations validate the Adiabatic Neural Network's capabilities for storage-free data processing and stochastic gradient descent, and the results suggest the Adiabatic Neural Network's potential to integrate computing and memory functions, making it an innovative solution to the von Neumann architecture bottleneck.

This study investigates the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, with the focus on the chiral magnetic effect. We apply a first-order expansion of the QCD sum rule in the polarization variable and derive a new hadron-to-quark mapping tailored to spin-polarized matter and the presence of the magnetic field. By incorporating the BEM mapping into the analysis, we obtain an equation of state for polarized strange quark matter and the corresponding mass spectrum for this system. The results obtained for the mass spectrum, such as the approximate linear relationship between hadron mass and quark mass, as well as the approximate slope of 1GeV, are consistent with experimental observations. The research also reveals that increasing the magnetic field strength leads to a decrease in hadron mass, with an estimated reduction of approximately 100MeV at a 10^19 Gauss field strength. The chiral partner states of Kaon and eta mesons, in particular, exhibit a narrowing of the mass splitting by around 50MeV due to the magnetic field.

A cubic graph is classified as even-2-factorable, or E2F for short, if it possesses an spanning 2-factor with an even number of edges. A recent discovery shows that every bipartite graph is classified as E2F. A new characterization of E2F graphs has been made in this study. A necessary and sufficient condition has been established to determine whether a graph with no bridge is classified as E2F. A backtracking algorithm has also been developed to convert any given graph into an E2F graph by adding edges. Finally, a new parameter called the E2F index has been introduced to measure the minimum number of additional edges required to transform a graph into an E2F graph.

Using the Bateman-Horn Conjecture proposed by S. M. Bateman and R. D. Horn, my objective is to provide a more precise estimation for the density of prime numbers generated by certain quadratic polynomials $ax^2+bx+c$ with $a>0$ and $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$. To achieve this, I'll utilize Li's adjustment to the Bateman-Horn Conjecture and distinguish the cases where $a$ is either square-free or has square factors.

Recent research has shown that Timeloops can slow down the execution of malware written in compiled languages, but a challenge remains for interpreting-based malware like PHP or Python. Since these types of malware run on a slower Python or PHPOPC VM, the technique of inserting delays via Timeloops loops may have a negligible impact. To address this issue, we have successfully created Timeloops modules for PHP and Python that utilize data structures like linked lists, hash maps, recursion, and sorting to increase overhead. By doing so, we have achieved at least a 100x performance reduction for each of these types, without compromising correctness or raising memory usage. Furthermore, we have shown that the Timeloops module for PHP can be easily integrated into the existing codebase, and for Python, it can be added as an imported module.

We suggest a new type of dark matter interaction mediated by a scalar meson that forms due to a new global symmetry breaking, akin to the breakdown of chiral symmetry in QCD. In this context, a generic class of models emerges where the dark matter behaves as a pseudo-Goldstone boson, which we examine in detail for an approach called the Linear Sigma Model. For instances where the dark matter possesses a complex phase in its transformation under the broken symmetry, we observe its elastic scattering with nucleons, which generally occurs through a low-energy theorem interaction and can be modeled by an effective nucleon-dark matter scattering length. In this framework, effective interaction parameters such as the nucleon mass, the broken symmetry decay constant, and the nucleon coupling to the broken symmetry current define the scattering process. In the Linear Sigma Model, this involves the interaction between two different sigma fields, which we examine in detail for the case where the dark matter is a pseudo-axion-like particle, a model that predicts the dark matter interaction with nucleons in terms of the effective parameter $f_{A\chi}\approx 10^{9}$ GeV. In this model, the dark matter interaction with nucleons is modulated by a linear derivative of the nucleon axial current, with the coupling constant falling within the range of 0.01-0.1 axion nucleon axial charges. As a result, the mass of the dark matter in this model lies within the 0.

This study develops an undetected target tracking approach, suitable for sensors with restricted viewing angles. It takes into account individual sensor restrictions and straightforward undetected target movement characteristics. Building upon finite state space Markov decision processes, optimal decision-making strategies are defined to minimize a steady-state undetected target probability. A simplified decision-making approach is also proposed. Analysis of the probability Markov decision process reveals that while the computational complexity generally escalates in relation to target position, it remains manageable for targets with short movement ranges. Theoretical and practical target tracking evidence support the effectiveness and efficiency of both optimal and undetected target tracking performance. Notably, performance is akin to that of a highly efficient state space magnitude. It falls within a manageable range, specifically (2\*|S| + 1) + O(|S| + |A| + |A||S|) + O(|A||S|) operations per iteration for value iteration, where |S| and |A| denote the state and action set sizes respectively. An optimization technique further reduces the calculation to quadratic order, making it more efficient. It requires only O(|A||S|) operations per iteration.

This research focuses on a highly observability-controlled reactivity problem for a non-linear variant of the fractional diffusion equation, featuring a source term and non-linear boundary conditions. It's shown that an observability inequality can be derived, which in turn manages an extinction phenomenon as described by a fractional-diffusion equation, considering localized measurements over a specific time frame. It also handles non-linear control and flux conditions. The results obtained apply to the case of time-periodic solutions to the non-linear control problem. A key step in the proof involves linearizing the problem within a suitable functional space, utilizing a global unique continuity theorem for the associated integral equation, and applying a unique null controllability property to a related linear non-homogeneous problem with unique source term regularity. The established theorem for non-linear reachability or extinction relies upon the regularity and observability properties for a related homogeneous problem with linearized source term.

This work proposes a groundbreaking application of Reinforcement Learning to the complex challenge of playing soccer against an opponent. By incorporating our manually controlled soccer game simulator, we have developed a novel approach to training policy networks that mimics real player behavior. The innovative method we outline in this research yields a learning algorithm capable of strategically fouling, sending the ball out of play, and even scoring goals. The breakthrough lies in the fact that these actions were not explicitly programmed but emerged naturally from the network's self-learning process. The novel method we introduce outperforms a basic Q-learning alternative by achieving a significantly higher score of 225-0 in ten test games, in contrast to the 2-0 result of the previous method in the same period. The research was made possible by open access to our publicly accessible game simulator, which was a key enabler in our successful experimentation.

This paper proposes an approach called adjoint-state full waveform inversion (AS-FWI) which utilizes complex-valued time-domain wavefields to generate simple-wavefield-based images (SWBIs). The challenge with AS-FWI is its vulnerability to local minima convergence due to the employment of time-domain wavefields. To circumvent this limitation, we suggest an alternative method based on the full waveform inversion in the frequency domain (FW-FWI). In this approach, we perform FW-FWI in the frequency domain (FWD) to generate an image in the spatial domain (SID). The key difference between SWBIs and the model in the spatial domain (MID) is that SWBIs are composed of both real and imaginary components, whereas MID has only a single component. To address this discrepancy, we suggest an optimization algorithm that only considers the component with the largest magnitude. The proposed algorithm is called the maximum-adjacent optimization (MAO) which generates the MID by aggregating the corresponding component from SWBIs. The MAO is shown to be effective in producing accurate MIDs from SWBIs generated by FWD. The results of numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in generating accurate MIDs from SWBIs generated by FWD. The experiments include synthetic seismic data and real field data, the latter of which shows the ability of the proposed approach to generate accurate MIDs even in the presence of significant noise. We've developed a comprehensive mathematical framework to analyze linear resonators strongly linked to a reservoir of linear elements. Based on this analysis, we've created an all-optical device that functions as a unidirectional passage for light or a quasi-circulator. This type of device allows light to flow in one direction or a specific direction among multiple channels while blocking the reverse path. The unique properties of these devices can be manipulated by adjusting the characteristics of the resonators and their connection to light sources. Furthermore, the device's response to light in different directions varies due to the chiral nature of the inter-resonator connection. All the properties of these devices can be precisely controlled because the resonators' characteristics can be adjusted using electrical means. The theoretical framework we've created has been verified experimentally and the results obtained match the predictions made from our analysis.

We have conducted an in-depth investigation of the IGR J19294+1816 source's 2019 high-intensity burst. During this event, the source exhibited a dual-humped spectrum with distinct features across both peaks. The lower energy range displayed soft spectrum characteristics, while the high count rate range above 10 counts s$^{-1}$ was scrutinized spectrally and temporally. The analysis revealed three distinct hardness intervals at 2.1, 10.4, and 13.4 s, alongside the detection of QPO signals at 1.04 and 0.93 Hz with significance levels of 3$\sigma$ and 2$\sigma$ respectively in the 10.4 s high count rate interval. Furthermore, the study of the source's 2019 flare demonstrated a similarity in temporal and spectral behavior to its 2015 flare.

We investigate the dynamics of an asymmetric noisy voting model where two political species compete, depending on their relative sizes. The model incorporates random fluctuations as well as irreversible changes in opinion when a minority individual switches sides. In low-noise scenarios, the model exhibits three distinct behaviors: the more numerous species dominating, the less numerous species prevailing, or coexistence of both. Our research extends this by examining how intermediate and exclusive zones shift with spatial and noise variations, alongside analyzing Cox processes describing the occurrence of opinion changes and exact expressions for Cox process rates in Cox-distribution contexts.

Citizen science is a concept that aligns with the principles of open science by allowing ordinary people to participate in scientific research. The use of Google Maps in citizen science projects exemplifies how public data can support collaborative and cooperative endeavors. Indonesia boasts a vast array of historic sundials, yet there is limited documentation and study of these features. The main challenge in documenting and analyzing Indonesian sundials lies in the country's expansive geographical area. To tackle this challenge, a crowdsourcing approach was undertaken to create an interactive map of Indonesian sundials. The project involved the participation of 1,051 users who contributed a total of 143 entries, with 127 entries proving to be unique. The final outcome, the Sundial Indonesia map, serves as the world's most comprehensive documentation and study of these timekeeping features. The project highlights how the Google Maps platform can facilitate the global collaboration required to map cultural heritage sites. Furthermore, it identifies potential risks and challenges that the platform may present in such endeavors.

This paper addresses an advanced scenario in which a base station, with limited energy, must manage complex data and energy transfers to multiple users simultaneously acting as data recipients and battery-powered devices. In this energy-constrained system that also transmits data, we introduce two novel concepts: joint data and energy transfers from a base station, and wireless charging via power lines. To analyze this system, we develop a superposition transmission model that accounts for energy consumption due to charge leakage. Our main goal is to maximize the total data transferred to all users, subject to energy constraints for both the base station and its power line, as well as total data rate requirements for each user. We propose a timing division multiple access-based scheme called TFET that facilitates joint data and energy transfers, and provide theoretical bounds on the total data transferred. Our findings reveal that in certain power line scenarios, a simplified approach can achieve near-optimal results, outperforming traditional multiuser MIMO techniques due to the power line's high loss rate. Through simulations, we evaluate the performance of joint data and energy transfers, observing notable data gains for each user compared to separate transfers.

The telework mandates of recent years have accelerated the automation of scientific experimental arrangements by adding long-distance remote operation capabilities to them. Since then, numerous studies have been published on the advantages of remote and robotic testing procedures. However, many research projects address only specific aspects of experimental tasks. This paper aims to generalize our previous findings by presenting an extensive framework that encompasses the full complexity of typical scientific experiments. This framework is then applied to derive prominent examples, such as the experiments carried out by the DANCE and DIAMOND-2 projects.

Developing a universal design framework for electrostatic phase plates is a key objective, encompassing parameters such as voltage, fill-factor, and pixel pattern in a two-dimensional array. To address this challenge, a computer-based simulation tool was created to evaluate various plate configurations by modeling the interaction between plates and electron beams. The tool's capabilities were demonstrated through the development of optimized designs that minimize probe size and adapt an existing multi-zone plate to reduce probe size. Additionally, the tool was used to design a plate with a unique pixel pattern that maximizes current density at the probe's center, modify a plate to incorporate this feature while maintaining minimal probe size, and design a zone-plate that concentrates current density at multiple focal points while compensating for distortion.

Unsupervised multilingual understanding (MU) is being explored for low-resource languages that lack annotated data, with a focus on comparing current attention-based models (RNNs and transformers) across various world regions. Our comprehensive study assesses 12 models across 87 tasks using world knowledge and dialog act prediction tasks with 1.1 million samples, as well as subjective user feedback from 20 participants. Our analysis reveals that RNN-based architectures outperform transformer models globally and in most world knowledge and dialog act prediction tasks. Although the best-performing model is a small transformer, its marginal gains over the best RNN baseline are not statistically significant. We also discover no correlation between model performance and world knowledge task accuracy when comparing RNN and transformer models, as well as a link between user preference and world knowledge. User feedback indicates that MU scores are influenced by both world knowledge and dialog acts, suggesting a need for better transformer models that can effectively capture dialog acts without introducing confusion.

Understanding a dynamic environment and building a cohesive map from visual place recognition data is a crucial step for creating maps from visual input. This process is complicated by changes in appearance due to factors like movement, weather, and time of day. We present a loop closure detection system based on RNN-based visual place recognition that can identify closed loops in these fluctuating conditions and thereby enhance the accuracy of maps generated from visual data. By training an attention module within an RNN network to prioritize invariant visual features, the model learns to focus on time-of-day and weather-related changes, outperforming other loop closure and 3D map generation systems, particularly in challenging scenarios. However, this enhanced detection capability comes with reduced detection rates in scenarios involving time of day changes.

YouTube's popularity as a streaming platform is largely attributed to its advanced quality management systems, including those utilizing cloud infrastructure, which ensure a consistent user experience. Our research on the effects of cloud infrastructure on video quality of service is complemented by an analysis of the impact of edge servers on video compression, allowing for more efficient scaling based on user device capabilities. Our analysis reveals that utilizing cloud infrastructure, including edge servers, to provide video quality can result in significant reductions in bitrate, potentially saving up to 50%, and also leads to a substantial decrease in energy consumption, making streaming more environmentally friendly.

We explore the unique quantum phenomena that emerge in graphene sheets after introducing charge carriers, particularly the renormalized quasiparticle behavior and its impact on thermodynamic properties, focusing on renormalized velocity's effect on specific heat in doped graphene. Our calculations utilize the perturbation theory within the random phase approximation for both single- and double-doped graphene, incorporating the logarithmic velocity renormalization arising from carrier interactions. Notable results show that in one-doped graphene, renormalized velocity increases the specific heat in hole bands while decreasing it in electron bands, with opposite effects observed in one-doped boron substitution. However, two-doped graphene exhibits a reduced renormalization of the Fermi velocity, leading to a renormalized velocity nearly equal to its unrenormalized value and specific heat behavior mimicking that of noninteracting graphene.

Recent advances in text-to-speech synthesis have achieved impressive results in naturalness, yet they fall short in capturing a wide range of speech expressions, from calm to excited, and from singing to emotional. The MaskedSpeech system addresses this limitation by drawing on the concept of masking expression in human communication. By utilizing a parallel acoustic signal that provides additional context, MaskedSpeech is capable of producing more varied and expressive speech. What sets this system apart is its ability to use a single, unlabeled acoustic signal to encode speech expression, allowing listeners to perceive the synthesized speech as more natural and natural-like. By evaluating expression through both objective metrics and subjective listener perception, MaskedSpeech demonstrates significant improvement in naturalness and expressiveness when compared to a baseline TTS system, without sacrificing naturalness.

We investigate a solitary wave system in a single crystal lattice, which is governed by an anharmonic oscillator, and observe its behavior in a one-dimensional setting. This study extends to a infinite lattice and examines the balance between nonlinear and dispersive forces. Our analysis reveals that when the ratio of these two factors is near the minimum value, the solitary wave remains stable, while for any other value, the wave becomes unstable. Additionally, we construct a numerical scheme to demonstrate the existence of solitary waves and present examples to illustrate their stability properties.

The study of Q-balls in theories with multiple stabilizing symmetries is examined, where the author demonstrates the formation of Q-balls that break a subset of the symmetries by analyzing a particular model. The model includes two U(1) symmetries, where the scalar field acquires a vacuum expectation value, resulting in spontaneous breaking of one of the symmetries. The study also explores the possibility of realizing the electroweak scale as the "inner" scale of a "high-scale" Q-ball, known as a FIP solution, in beyond Standard Model (BSM) scalar theories. Furthermore, the possibility of baryon number violation within such Q-balls is addressed, where it is demonstrated that such behavior is possible, potentially leading to a link between "outer" baryon number violation and the generation of a baryon asymmetry in the early universe.

A universe model that is cyclic in nature and excludes a big crunch event is examined, applying the principle of holographic dark energy. By employing the hetrogeneity approach, we analyze the model's dynamics. Research into a single-scale, cyclic universe model is conducted, drawing on the concept of a cutoff $\Lambda$ that is determined by the total size and structure of the universe. Specifically, we explore the impact of the Granda-Oliveros cutoff on the model, as it is capable of adapting to the changing conditions of the expanding and contracting phases, based on the parameters $\sqrt{\Omega_k}$, $D$, and $c$ that define the entropy within a single-scale, cyclic universe. Without consideration of the entropy within a cutoff volume, a single-scale, cyclic universe model suggests that the universe's cycle duration is limited by the constraints of the cosmological constant and dark energy, as these factors dictate the Hubble parameter's value, which in turn limits the cycle time to approximately $10^{10}$ years. By incorporating a more flexible cutoff volume, a cycle time of approximately $10^{100}$ seconds is obtained, allowing the model to accommodate the age of the cosmic microwave background, which is $10^{17}$ seconds. The model also demonstrates the possibility of using the entropy within a cutoff volume to explain the origin of the baryon asymmetry, the generation of primordial black holes during the contracting phase, and the avoidance of

A function similar to the Riemann zeta function can be defined for any graph, and this definition shares key properties with the original zeta function. When a graph has a regular covering, we demonstrate that a covering zeta function can be related to the original zeta zeta function using a simple formula. Additionally, we use this relationship to express the covering zeta function in terms of the original graph's laplace transform.
This paper describes an innovative approach to assigning a finite non-abelian extension to any given additive Galois module that is highly ramified over the rational numbers.

The search for invisible decays of neutral particles with extended lifespans is being intensively pursued at present and upcoming high-energy collider facilities. Due to the wide range of particles with varying lifespans, the optimal search approach varies between them. We propose a unified, adaptive search methodology, centered on a specific particle decay length. This methodology, adaptable to different regimes, can be easily applied across a wide spectrum of particle lifespan durations. We demonstrate its advantages by employing it to address the micro-black hole search at the Large Hadron Collider, yielding micro-black hole findings that are relevant to both scientists and engineers.

The number of factors that influence a speaker's word choice during speech varies, ranging from one as constant background to over 4,000 that are highly dynamic as individuals adjust their speech to fit the situation. Although recent studies have shown that context can significantly impact the interpretation of semantic changes in language, it's the lack of a comprehensive understanding of how contextual fluctuations impact interpretation that remains. This research aims to provide such an in-depth analysis and the findings demonstrate the effect of contextual variability on interpretation is quite pronounced, with a significant effect size of 0.89, indicating a standard deviation of 2.89, which exceeds 2 times the vocabulary standard error. Models of dynamic semantic composition that account for the variability of contextual input align well with this result, whereas the impact of a variable context on interpretation is often underestimated, as shown by the 0.19 standard error provided by the English language.

We investigated the properties of ultra-light particles that could serve as dark matter, focusing on how they affect dwarf galaxies and the stability of those galaxies over time. Specifically, we examined the relationship between the mass and self-interaction constant of these particles in relation to observed properties of dwarf galaxies and gravitational wave constraints, as well as nuclear stability and decay products in milk way satellites. Additionally, we determined the minimum mass of these particles relative to their number density in order to prevent them from dominating the dark matter composition, and found that in some cases, they could only exist as subdominant dark matter with a density ratio of at least one part in a million.

The organization of functional neural tissues largely depends on the intricate dynamics of nuclear migration during retinogenesis. To gain a clearer understanding of nuclear migration in retinogenesis, we developed a statistical model that analyzes the distribution of nuclei within the retinal lamination. By extracting key features from lamellar images and constructing an energy function that accounts for inter-nuclear forces, we are capable of replicating the observed features and deriving a time-dependent model of nuclear migration. A comparative analysis of our model against live-cell time-lapse data reveals that the overall accuracy of our simulation can be improved by including the effects of retinal expansion and varying nuclear sizes. Furthermore, the model provides insights into the relative importance of specific nuclear traits that govern their positioning within the retina, which in turn reflects the functional requirements of retinogenesis.

In image reconstruction within compressed sensing, a sub-sampled system of linear equations is employed to recover an image from incomplete measurements, with various optimization methods such as OMP, COORDATE, and FISTA being commonly applied. The effectiveness of these algorithms heavily relies on the relationship between the original and observed data points, particularly their mutual coherence. This study proposes a mutual coherence-minimal transformation algorithm to enhance the mutual coherence of the transformation matrix, ultimately improving the reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis is provided to support the idea that a lower mutual coherence translates to a reduced upper bound of reconstruction error. Both simulated experiments and real-world tests confirm that the proposed algorithm yields more accurate results than conventional approaches. Additionally, a discussion on how the algorithm's performance scales with the number of observed data points and the level of added noise is included.

We've developed a theoretical framework to model active systems in dimensions between 2 and 5 based on hydrodynamics theory. Our approach diverges from linearized hydrodynamics by incorporating mean field non-equilibrium dynamics and is applicable to a variety of systems, including flocks of birds, microbial swarms, and tumor growth. In these intermediate dimensions, we discovered that systems exhibit power law scaling with a dimensionality parameter 'd' and demonstrate quasi-long range order. Notably, in one-dimensional spaces, we found that standard hydrodynamic theory fails to capture the non-equilibrium nature of self-propelled systems due to broken isotropy. Our model also shows that in three-dimensional spaces, systems exhibit equilibrium-like behavior and that the non-equilibrium character of flow defects can be observed. Our predictions can be tested by analyzing the relationship between the velocity and the gradient of the orientation in systems characterized by topological defects.

This research aims to address the escalating threat of phishing in institutional communications, particularly in high-tech sectors, such as academic research. To tackle this issue, we collected a vast dataset of up to one million historical email addresses from MIT, utilizing MIT's extensive network infrastructure. To process this dataset, we developed an open-source Python tool called mitmbox. It enables the extraction of past email addresses from institutional servers by emulating legitimate administrative actions, utilizing existing network infrastructure. Our implementation included the creation of custom features, such as frequency distribution and domain statistics, enabling us to analyze mailing patterns. We hope that by providing researchers with access to this large-scale dataset and the mitmbox tool, we will aid in the development of more effective, content-based anti-phishing systems.

The recent discovery of a temperature-driven electronic phase transition in cuprates, characterized by a zero-temperature Lifshitz signal, remains unexplained due to the absence of a closing energy gap in their band structures. By constructing a two-dimensional Hubbard model, we demonstrate that adding hole pockets at the (0,0) and (pi,0) regions of the Fermi surface leads to a volume-driven Lifshitz transition. A detailed analysis of correlations within the model reveals that this transition produces strong CDW, pairing, and self-energy singularities, potentially accounting for high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the appearance of hole pockets and the observed properties of the parent compound, and we predict that a volume-driven Lifshitz transition can account for the material's scattering and superconducting properties.

To enhance the detection efficiency of low-energy neutrons in the liquid scintillator, 1000 ppm of Neoprobe Gd-NOP is added as a neutron capture agent, effectively multiplying the original neutron detection efficiency by roughly ten. By taking into account the varying compositions of GS2 mixture and neutron energy spectra, approximately $10^4$ additional low-energy neutrons are anticipated to be detected. Notably, these additional detections primarily result from improved efficiency within the same neutron energy bins, with only one bin showing a shift in flux due to the added Gd.

This paper develops the minimax principle for a class of functionals whose underlying topology is jointly weaker in its compact and continuous components. The established variational theory leverages key properties of a linking family within the context of weakly compact sets in a locally convex topological vector space. Furthermore, the article demonstrates its results through multiple applications, including the study of minimal geodesics on a manifold with finite curvature, the discovery of periodic orbits on a compact manifold, and the proof of compactness for a set defined by a condition for minimal elements.

Recent observations reveal a strong correlation between star systems, highlighting the necessity to examine exoplanetary diversity in relation to host star properties across various categories, from stellar activity to system formation. Recent advances in data visualization and statistical modeling facilitate a comprehensive overview of large datasets by presenting data in a unified, low-dimensional space that captures both star system properties and exoplanetary features. When visualizing a specific category of data, such as stellar activity, each point represents a specific star system and its associated exoplanetary system, with color-coded points indicating host star characteristics and points' shapes and sizes reflecting exoplanetary characteristics. Employing this approach, we illustrate the complex relationship between star systems and demonstrate the significant influence of star systems on planetary architectures, beyond just host star categories, and the substantial effect on planetary radii, caused by stellar activity, is evident from the mapping of systems without and with active stars. We propose a flexible, open-source framework for creating such star system maps, with the potential to uncover hidden correlations in future datasets, especially as data from missions like PLATO and ELPS approach.

To improve efficiency and consistency in processing and understanding of data, Networked
Intelligence is applied to text extraction from ID cards. Initially, we outline the
process of applying NLP to this text extraction procedure, highlighting the key
advantages this approach offers. Our experimental results show that NLP-based
methods excel at text extraction, leading to increased accuracy and processing
consistency. To further enhance the results, we developed a novel n-gram
modification strategy that leverages the network capabilities of Networked
Intelligence. This strategy is proven effective at improving the n-gram
representations required for ID card processing. Our findings demonstrate a
significant improvement in the mBERT model's performance, leading to better
accuracy and robustness in the processing pipeline.

A new approach has been developed to study driven quantum systems under time-periodic Hamiltonians, particularly for systems that can be described by coherent states. Within this framework, the Hamiltonian is expressed as an operator polynomial in annihilation and creation operators, making it applicable to a diverse range of driven systems including those with time-volkov states. The use of the chiral phase space allows the framework to apply to both genuinely quantum systems and classical systems described by Hamiltonian dynamics that are periodic. The method retains crucial symmetries of the original Hamiltonian and enables the precise determination of energy and quasi-momentum for various driven systems. The method's effectiveness was further validated by applying it to specific examples, such as the Jahn-Tune model and multi-photon sidebands in driven cavities, revealing the existence of resonances that lead to quasi-periodic behavior.

Our analysis of the detected asteroids reveals compelling proof of consistent rotational acceleration. The acceleration rates fall within plausible bounds set by physical limits, and statistical analyses show that the data aligns with the hypotheses of accelerated rotation (p=0.27) and isotropic acceleration (p=0.18). The acceleration rates vary widely among the asteroids, with some experiencing significant changes in rotational period, such as increasing from over 10 hours to less than four hours within a year. The acceleration appears to be confined to smaller asteroids, with those under three kilometers in diameter showing significant accelerations, while larger asteroids primarily exhibit negligible acceleration. The magnitude of acceleration exceeds what can be attributed to the YORP effect in the observed system, implying that the PYP effect may produce significantly different outcomes compared to our own solar system due to the unique characteristics of the PSR J2032+36 being a millisecond pulsar with high photon energy and temperature.

The evolution of online communities is heavily influenced by individual behavior and actions. Online forums serve as important spaces for community development and the expression of diverse opinions. Our research focuses on the community structure of online political forums, examining the structure and connectivity of Swedish political discussions within the /pol/ community on 4chan. By applying a approach that considers individual posting history, we observed that community membership is not static, with individuals frequently shifting between communities based on the discussion topic. The likelihood of a political discusser returning to a specific community is affected by the reputation of that community, with the probability of return influenced significantly by previous negative interactions. Our research also reveals that interconnectedness between discussions is not confined to a specific scope, with cross-subcommunity connections occurring more frequently than expected. These findings contribute valuable knowledge to our understanding of online community dynamics, particularly within the context of political discussions.

Let X be a compact surface within a higher-dimensional surface D with non-positive curvature. Given a subgroup G that moves X and is not limited, we analyze the conditions for X to be singularly positioned relative to the orbits of G in D. If X has no special geometric features, X will occupy the entire surface and, if it has extensive movement, it will also fill the entire surface. However, if X has a specific type of curvature, it will only occupy a particular region and, if it has limited movement, it will be confined to a smaller part of the surface. Additionally, if a group has non-limiting movement, we identify the conditions under which it can be described as a product of rotation and scaling elements, and if it can be described in a more complex way, it can be broken down into simpler components through a process of reduction.

We present new data analysis of the LAMOST-MD dwarf samples to enhance our
understanding of low-mass stars. By deriving improved mass-radius relationships,
our study establishes a clearer framework for characterizing these stars. Through
analysis of the infrared flux from the TESS band, researchers can derive radii and
identify deviations from the established mass dwarf model. Additionally, our team
used existing data to derive dwarf star densities and established a revised mass-radius
relationship that accounts for the effects of magnetic fields. This enhanced model
can be applied to identify potential white dwarfs masquerading as mass dwarfs and is a
significant step towards more accurate characterization of these stars.

A new approach for creating line-based waves in the visible light spectrum using a ground plane with a graphene design has been demonstrated. By adjusting the thermal mode of graphene, these line waves can control electromagnetic conditions on a two-dimensional surface, enabling direct contactless temperature sensing and imaging. The performance of two types of configurations has been simulated and experimentally validated, demonstrating the feasibility of using optical line waves for precise, real-time temperature measurements and imaging applications.

We have developed a query framework that allows for efficient finding of objects
within structured data by incorporating comparisons between values and positions.
This framework is suitable for handling self-joins and can be applied to typical
database and graph queries. Our research focuses on identifying query characteristics
that ensure efficient evaluation using a specific evaluation cost measure. This measure
considered query results ordered according to the self-join evaluation tree and did
not permit reordering or reusing previously computed results. Our research has
identified sufficient conditions for determining feasible evaluation of queries with
self-joins, as well as necessary conditions in the case of binary, tree-shaped
queries. These necessary conditions can also be used for practical purposes. Additionally,
we have developed an algorithm to transform certain feaible queries into equivalent
forms without self-joins, enabling application of standard evaluation techniques.

We investigate the uncertainty in rational function continuity assessment, particularly its variant within the D_CP^1 complexity class, which determines the regions where a rational function is non-zero. We demonstrate that this uncertainty can be decided precisely using an alternating Turing machine with one unbounded memory unit, or alternatively using a specific type of cellular automaton with one infinite track. We also establish a comparable precise description for the uncertainty in real algebraic set membership, which depends on the underlying field's transcendental degree.

A new method has been developed to study the difference in polarization patterns between B^0 and B^0_s mesons when they decay into two charm mesons and a photon. This method uses the q^2 dependence of the polarization in virtual process, taking advantage of the distinct mass difference between B^0 and B^0_s mesons. To address potential uncertainties, a combination of techniques and inputs from LHCb and other experiments has been utilized to constrain the variation in d f^2 / d q^2 within the charmonium mass range. A likelihood analysis was performed to determine the polarization variation between B^0_s and B^0 mesons, resulting in a value of 1.19 with a variation of ±0.32 and a variation of ±0.1.
