Let $Q\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded domain with a smooth boundary $\partial Q$. For any integer $m \ge 2$, this paper proves the convergence of a high-order numerical method for solving time-dependent mean field games systems near the final time $T$. The mentioned numerical scheme achieves first-order convergence in time near $T$ with sufficient smoothness in $Q \times [0,T)$, and spatial convergence rates depend on the smoothness of functions within $\bar{Q}$. To begin, a Crandall-Lions type approximate system is created by modifying the original system of equations $m$ times near $T$. It is demonstrated that the solution to this approximate system remains uniformly bounded from below and above by continuous functions. Consequently, by applying the theorem of Barles and Souganidis, the barrier technique is utilized to show that the numerical solution converges to the semi-relaxed viscosity solution of the limiting system as the number of iterations approaches infinity.

The rapid advancement of machine learning, particularly deep learning, has revolutionized the way we process information and solve complex problems. However, these advancements have also highlighted a pressing need to address the lack of transparency in AI models. As a result, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has emerged to develop transparent AI models that can provide meaningful insights into their decision-making processes. Despite numerous existing research initiatives in XAI, current models still struggle to generate comprehensive and accurate explanations for their predictions. This study proposes a novel framework centered around the concept of feedback-enhanced explanation generation (FEG), which leverages user-generated feedback to produce more accurate and meaningful explanations for AI models' predictions. By integrating the existing related work, the proposed FEG framework can be applied to a range of applications, such as improving the performance of classification models by incorporating user-generated relevance signals into the model's optimization process. Our numerical results demonstrate the superiority of the FEG framework over traditional XAI methods in terms of model performance and provide a more robust and accurate basis for evaluating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

We have observed the unusual rotation profile of KIC 9267654 with the Kepler telescope, where its inertial frame period changes rapidly and unpredictably. This profile may be a result of magnetic activity or dynamos within the star. To evaluate this possibility, we analyzed the star's activity using various methods, including the bisector span technique, flare frequency, and rotation models. We found that the star is likely fully covered in spots or has a slow rotating equator with a faster rotating pole. However, a spot model with differential rotation does not account for line broadening. We also determined that the observed broadening can be explained by a distribution of spot inclinations. The star's surface features can cause line broadening, making it difficult to estimate its rotation velocity accurately. We suggest that future studies focus on estimating line broadening rather than rotation velocity, and that observing flare frequencies and chromospheric activity may provide a more reliable assessment of the star's dynamo activity.

Recently, there's been an increasing focus on using deep learning to identify misinformation and a significant push to detect fake news on social media. Traditional methods that rely solely on text or a combination of text and images often fall short in this task. Furthermore, advanced deep learning techniques can inadvertently promote the creation of more visually appealing misinformation. To overcome these limitations, we've developed MetaFEND, an innovative multi-modal fake news detection framework utilizing generative adversarial networks. As its name suggests, MetaFEND's goal is to predict and counteract misinformation effectively. At its core, MetaFEND employs text and visual feature generators that blend content with stylistic information to mimic the appearance of real articles. In an adversarial exchange, these generators are pitted against powerful classifiers, which strive to accurately categorize images and texts. Ultimately, this competition leads to the generation of visually compelling and factually accurate information that is harder to distinguish from genuine content. Experimental results show significant enhancements in fake news detection rates when using MetaFEND, with its source code publicly available at this link: https://github.com/zhengqian99/MetaFEND.

Consider a one-dimensional periodic transport equation with nonlocal flux and no dissipation mechanism. When started with smooth odd initial data, the study reveals that in the absence of diffusion, the system generates an infinite number of discontinuities in a short time, which accumulates near the spatial point $x=0$. To understand this phenomenon, we provide a precise condition for the emergence of singularities and illustrate it with an explicit example, which can be analyzed through the lens of a parabolic boundary value equation.

This study delves into auto-encoding (AoI) over networks, specifically examining systems operating on a discrete time scale and examining two scenarios for discrete time systems with exponential distributions and infinite queues. The paper derives the stationary AoI probability for systems where updating is guaranteed at each time step, as well as the mean stationary AoI in an infinite queue scenario. A comparison of continuous and discrete time systems reveals that the former's stationary AoI distribution does not directly correspond to the squared error of the latter's stationary AoI probabilities. Moreover, the paper investigates the impact of time-scale and queue-size on AoI probabilities in systems with exponential distributions, observing that increasing time-sync or queue-size results in a decrease in stationary AoI probabilities, a phenomenon that aligns with the principle of discrete renewal systems.

On a vector space V with an associated symmetric matrix C, we investigate the properties of admissible Drinfeld twists within the q-deformed context of Uq(gl(n)). Specifically, the twist lies within the quantized envelope algebra of V, denoted as Dq(Env(V)). Building upon prior work by Etingof and Khoroshkin (2000), the twist is constructed through a recursive process from the 'basic twist'. The construction process ensures the admissibility of the resulting Drinfeld twist under specific conditions, namely the rationality property with respect to the q-parameter and specific scaling by q-powers. The admissibility proof involves combining K-matrices through combinations of the adjoint and quantum permutation operators, and the rationality condition is satisfied by imposing specific constraints, namely the det(1-C) = 0 = det(1+C) = 0. The evaluation of these constraints leads to solutions in the form of admissible Drinfeld twists in the q-deformed context, and the solution set is shown to be in a one-to-one correspondence with certain subsets of integers. Additionally, the admissible Drinfeld twists in the classical context are shown to be in an n!/2-to-1 correspondence with ordered partitions of the set {1, 2, ..., n}.

Researchers have long studied quaternary Golay complementary pairs in the context of length-constraints, whether in one-dimensional or multi-dimensional settings. A key discovery emerged showing that for GCA pairs constructed in multi-dimensional settings, their lengths must be divisible by twelve. Another study has now expanded this research by proving that GCA pairs in lengths not divisible by twelve are indeed impossible for settings beyond two dimensions. This study also establishes a criterion for GCDAs in multi-dimensional settings at scale thirteen and offers an example of a GDC pair at this scale, also demonstratable in multi-dimensional settings.

The precise arrangement of dopants within an intrinsic silicon material is a key factor influencing its electronic properties and quantum behavior. In this context, researchers have been able to observe a shift in the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction by adjusting the placement of donor impurities within a silicon crystal. A photon blockade effect was also enabled, in a two-dimensional array of donor impurities in silicon-28, by carefully controlling the exchange interaction through opto-spin control. Furthermore, this effect's robustness against noise was found to be enhanced by increasing the donor array's doping density. Opto-spin blockades exhibit varying characteristics in one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, with the ability to tune at room temperature and beyond made possible by light. These findings make the exchange-controlled opto-spin system versatile for applications in near-infrared spin filtering and high-resolution spin spectroscopy.

We investigate a class of time-varying directed separation systems, including dynamic Bayesian networks and stochastic grammars, by analyzing time-series data. These systems belong to a broader category of time-sensitive sparse directed probabilistic grammars (PSDPs), which have raised concerns about their challenging inference and learning difficulties. However, we demonstrate that PSDPs can be viewed as generative models within the framework of linear programming, which not only simplifies their inference by reducing it to a linesearch but also enables the integration of powerful solver tools. This formulation's effectiveness in handling high-dimensional problems makes solving previously complex time-series applications, such bidirectional sequence labelling and multi-task sequence labelling, to their optimal solutions feasible and efficient.

In the realm of stable homotopy theory, we establish a polynomial ring structure on the graded ring $H_*(QX^+ \wedge QY^+)$. This structure incorporates and utilizes the concept of partitions within the double $Y \to Y \vee Y$. Notably, the properties of this ring structure provide a proof of the commutativity of $QX$-spaces, as the commutative and associative laws of the ring follow directly from the characteristics of stable polynomial rings and the interpretation of partitions.

Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been highly successful in automatic image analysis tasks, particularly in medical imaging where precise annotation is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Although effective, the performance of these models heavily depends on large, meticulously annotated datasets. This paper proposes a new transfer learning approach, called virtual annotation, to automatically generate initial annotations for real images based on previously annotated synthetic images. This method is particularly useful when the synthetic and real images share similar visual characteristics, allowing the CNN to generalize its training. The approach was successfully applied to two examples: generating MRI CT images and deforming synthetic ultrasound images with real patient data. In both cases, the automatic annotations served as accurate starting points for subsequent semi-supervised refinement, resulting in high-precision segmentations of target regions.

Research on quantum nonlocality in multipartite systems has made significant strides in recent years, particularly in demonstrating strong nonlocality in certain types of quantum states, such as those without local hidden variables (HLHMs). We investigated the capabilities of another class of quantum nonlocal states, specifically unextendible product bases (UPBs), to exhibit strong nonlocality in a new setting, where local measurements are limited to MHLHMs. We found that UPBs can indeed display strong nonlocality under these conditions, and provided an example of such a phenomenon in the case of five parties and two measurement outcomes. This discovery expands our understanding of the diverse range of local correlations that can be generated by quantum entanglement.

For upcoming large-scale spectroscopic surveys using optical routines, like DESI, there will be a significant number of robots in operation simultaneously. Ensuring their seamless functionality is essential for a successful survey. We've established a method for coordinating these robots through a market-based system that guarantees both safety and efficiency. Each robot is given autonomy to bid for the best trajectory that minimizes observation time, while also being able to place side bets for any collisions with other robots. Only the side bets with the highest confidence of causing a collision are executed, thus avoiding unnecessary interventions. We've tested this approach by determining the price and side bets for each possible time shift, enabling us to find the most favorable combination of parameters that avoids all collisions. This method proves effective in both laboratory settings and real-world scenarios with four DESI robots. We've also shown how to account for differences in processing times and the entry of new robots into the system dynamically. For a detailed explanation of this method, please refer to our accompanying paper which describes the same system in greater depth.

GP 2, an efficient programming model for high-performance computing on shared-memory systems, has seen a surge in interest due to the widespread adoption of multicore technology. To enhance GP 2 and address memory allocation issues on large-scale machines with limited memory banks, we developed a new data structure called BigArray. BigArray allows for the seamless allocation of memory exceeding a single bank, with minimal performance impact. In our tests, we observed that replacing the existing array array with BigArray yielded an 8-fold increase in throughput for a representative graph program (Isomorphism Testing) on a 240-core system, without significantly altering the programs in our evaluation suite. We have updated GP 2 to include BigArray as a built-in feature and updated the relevant codebase to demonstrate the potential benefits of this innovation.

Our proposal offers a unified approach to resolving the issue of relying on labeled data for training the feature learning module. This issue can be classified as either unsupervised or supervised feature learning, depending on the availability of labels. To tackle this problem, we introduce a versatile framework that incorporates confidence labels to distinguish between samples with and without labels. Initially addressed in the context of unsupervised classification, the framework now also resolves the issue of supervised classification. By formulating the problem as an implicit confidence prediction process, the framework uses contrastive learning to resolve the issue of unsupervised classification, while employing a confidence-aware contrastive learning objective to resolve the issue of supervised classification. To further enhance the model's performance, we introduce two additional modules, the confidence label learning module and the module for refining the confidence labels after sampling, both of which incorporate the confidence labels into the feature learning process. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving impressive results on the market leader dataset for text-based 3D shape retrieval and other retrieval datasets. Our source code is available online at this link: https://github.com/zhengzhengzhengzheng/CIAL.

We've created unlimited number of infinite sequences of graphs that are limitless in their symmetry through an intricate process. In doing so, two new sequences of graphs have been found that possess infinite symmetry by combining a special type of graph known as a circulant graph with another sequence of graphs that are graphs of linear growth and exhibit symmetry.

A recent extension of the Group Lasso was developed, specifically designed to handle both continuous and categorical groups of coefficients within the estimation of a large-scale regression model. This novel approach not only achieves effective model compression and efficient variable selection but also guarantees that the resulting model remains interpretable. The group Lasso formulation's complexity was proven to be non-convex, yet efficient non-linear solvers were derived and demonstrated through numerical experiments to outperform established methods, particularly in scenarios involving the removal of superfluous groups of coefficients from the model.

Recent developments in question-answering systems have been positively impacted by the creation of factual knowledge graphs, which provide a source of reliable information and a training data that preserves semantic connections between words. Despite these advancements, little research has been done to improve knowledge graph-based models' ability to understand complex sentences and infer meanings. Our work aims to enhance such models by incorporating pretrained language model components that bridge the gap between the simple semantic connections preserved in knowledge graphs and the intricate linguistic patterns found in text. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach by showing significant improvements in sentence-level task performance on two datasets, including a newly introduced subset that contains near-synonymous expressions in TREC. The results of our study also suggest the potential of knowledge graph-based pretraining as a viable option for models intended to analyze large quantities of unstructured text.

This study explores the connection between nonlocal diffusion models and classical PDE models as their transition occurs, examining how the kernel's approach to locality affects model parameters and exponents in the limit. A key finding indicates that under certain rescaling, the nonlocal model's limit involves a fractional Laplacian with a specific rescaling of the normalization constant. Conversely, rapid rescaling leads to a classical local diffusion equation with a uniquely determined rescaling of the density normalization. These discoveries underscore the significance of accounting for nonlocal normalization when modeling biological systems with nonlocal interactions.

Traditional panoramic stitching methods rely on aligning features across images, a process enhanced by incorporating inertial measurement unit (IMU) data. Although effective, this approach demands expensively equipped cameras. By introducing a novel, accessibly implementable approach that leverages the high-frequency sensor readings of IMUs, the research team has developed a prior that guides a learning algorithm to build a panoramic view from a single viewpoint. Utilizing a generative model that generates features from the IMU-derived motion data, the approach significantly reduces the computational burden, allowing for real-time application on standard processors. Moreover, the method enhances robustness to varying motion conditions, a common challenge in traditional methods. The approach surpasses the state-of-the-reach methods in terms of accuracy, as verified by real-world experiments and quantitative assessments.

This study examines specific cosets of the Weyl group in conjunction with degenerate Eisenstein series, focusing on the root system $\mathfrak{sl}(n+1)$ within $\mathfrak{sl}(n+1)$ representations. We establish that certain cosets of the Weyl group cause these series to reduce to zero for the Lie group $SL(n+1,\mathbb{R})$. Additionally, we have derived an explicit formula indicating the annihilation of the series by specific elements of the Weyl group, and this formula aligns with earlier findings by Flath and Gelfand for $SL(n+,\mathbb{R})$. This work extends their results by addressing a broader set of cosets in the Weyl group.

Modeling complex systems such as brain dynamics through mathematical equations
has proven to be a powerful analytical tool, which can also aid in understanding
and developing effective treatments for conditions like Parkinson's Disease.
Although significant progress has been made in creating computational models of
neural activity, a key challenge lies in incorporating realistic parameter values.
We suggest leveraging existing experimental datasets to refine these models,
emphasizing a data-driven approach known as simultaneous spectrogram optimization.
This method minimizes the difference between the model's output and real-world
measurements, reflecting both individual and collective behavior. We demonstrate
its effectiveness for Parkinson's Disease treatment through a mock dataset, and
suggest its applicability to real patients by including neural activity patterns
extracted from local recordings. The resulting optimal treatments yield realistic
parameter values, highlighting simultaneous spectrogram optimization's potential
to inform clinical interventions and enhance parkinsonian model cure discovery.

This study introduces a novel approach to rendering vector graphics with tapered ends, addressing the limitations of current join and end methods that rely on simple perpendicular extensions. To enhance performance, a streamlined algorithm is implemented using GPU-based triangulation for smooth tapered effects. Additionally, an alternative GPU-based method with precise diagonal line projection is proposed to match the overall shape accuracy of traditional rendering. Benchmark tests demonstrate the current algorithm's superior efficiency in balancing visual quality and performance.

The recent discoveries of powerful outflows in galaxies, driven by supermassive black holes merging, offer a fresh perspective on the co-evolution of galaxies and their central black holes. These observations highlight the significant impact of energetic outflows, which carry away mass and energy, potentially influencing the evolution of galaxies by regulating the consumption of gas and the expulsion of heavy elements. To understand this phenomenon better, researchers have developed analytical models of galaxy evolution, incorporating observations of radial velocities of outflows and their effects on the consumption and enrichment of heavy elements in galaxies. The results of these models show that the consumption of gas and the accumulation of heavy elements are influenced by the balance between the outflows driving material away from the galaxy and the inflows pulling material back in. Further, researchers have discovered that galaxy mergers play a crucial role in re-cycling enriched gas, allowing it to fall back into the galaxy and contribute to the synthesis of new generations of stars. A new, observational index has been proposed to quantify the ratio of outflows to inflows, which can inform galaxy evolution models and be used in conjunction with super-Eddington accretion to constrain the consumption of gas and the synthesis of new generations of stars.

A new type of radial basis function interpolation has been proposed with an underlying Gaussian exponential function. We investigate the characteristics of this quasi-interpolation formula, demonstrating its ability to preserve convexity and monotonicity, as well as linear precision. Additionally, we examine its performance in curve smoothing, resulting in a smooth curve without oscillations.

Deep Learning frameworks, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have excelled at solving complex computer vision problems. The success of these models largely depends on their ability to generalize well from limited training data. To achieve high accuracy, it's crucial to have access to vast amounts of diversified samples. However, obtaining such large-scale datasets is often impractical due to the extensive manual effort required for annotation. In response, this research proposes a novel annotation method called mask-based data augmentation. By artificially expanding the dataset through the use of super pixel delimiting masks, the method aims to enhance the performance of CNNs. The idea behind this approach is that using Delimiting Masks as a form of data augmentation can help the CNNs learn more robust features, even when applied to complex tasks such as image classification. To validate the effectiveness of this method, the study utilized the OpenImages dataset and compared the results of training CNNs with and without delimiting masks. The outcome showed a significant improvement in accuracy, with the model using delimiting masks achieving a 1.5% increase in accuracy. To further investigate the mechanism behind this improvement, the research also employed techniques such as Grad-CAM and a statistical analysis of feature maps, along with an analysis of the impact of training delimiting masks on the robustness of CNNs.

Speech enhancement is a challenging task in both domain-specific and cross-domain scenarios due to various acoustic disturbances. Recent studies have shown that convolution recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) are highly effective at extracting both temporal and spectral features from speech spectrograms. Building on this foundation, we propose a novel network architecture called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which incorporates a mask prediction module to map input enhanced spectrograms to the original target speech. The DPCRN leverages a dual-path design that allows it to process speech spectrograms in the time-frequency domain by employing CRNNs to capture temporal dependencies and multi-layer dilated convolution layers to model local spectral dependencies within each frame. Furthermore, we introduce two types of cross-layer multi-layer perceptrons called the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and the global maximum pooling (GMP) to facilitate the exchange of global maximum pooling features between the two network paths. Experimental evaluations on public benchmark datasets ST2021 and CSS2021 demonstrate the superiority of the DPCRN over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of its design in capturing temporal and local spectral dependencies, as well as the ability of the mask prediction module to refine the enhanced spectrograms by correcting artifacts.

The effective field theory (EFT) of dark energy introduces numerous functions of time and scale that characterize the interplay between dark energy and dark matter on small cosmic scales. To determine the final functions that break this symmetry, the turn-around radii of massive dark matter structures serve as turnaround boundaries. By using a likelihood analysis of the turnaround radii and their expansion rates from the DESI and Euclid missions along with the cluster count from the KIDS-$5000$ telescope, researchers found the BOM and TOM models of DCDM to be favored at over $3\sigma$ confidence levels. These models exhibit a distinct turn-around radii distribution, easily distinguishable from the $\Lambda$CDM model, making them potential targets for future missions like Euclid and DESI. Additionally, the analysis indicates that these models break the dark sector degeneracy with a postively running DE initial conditions, making them an excellent example of self-accelerating dark energy models with a suitable DE potential.

A newly proposed, uncomplicated two-fluid model of turbulence is evaluated against established turbulence theories and a broad range of numerical simulations. The model accurately forecasts the dependence of heat transfer on the precision of numerical simulations, as well as the energy spectrum and decay of turbulent flows, across various conditions and in three-dimensional and two-dimensional representations. When applied to Rayleigh-B\'enard convection, it successfully predicts the increase in heat transfer with increasing numerical simulations, as well as the behavior of the energy spectrum and decay of turbulent flows, in three various regimes, including one where heat transfer scales linearly with numerical simulations, in two power laws of one $1/2$ and one $3/4$, and one with an exponential increase. The model attributes this linear regime to dominant shear flow, whereas the two power law regimes are explained by the strength of turbulent cascades. Notably, it also shows that the linear regime emerges at a specific threshold of numerical simulations, approximately $10^9$, in line with prior research. The model also reveals that the $k^{-3}$ peak in the energy spectrum corresponds to the two coexisting currents, a $k^{-5/3}$ peak to the turbulent cascade, and a $k^{-1}$ current to the shear flow. The model also offers a straightforward explanation for the decline in the position of the peak in the energy spectrum as the numerical simulations increase. In relation to the heat transfer, the two-regime view of the model is consistent

We investigate the potential for creating entanglement among multiple particles using a shared interaction with one that is not part of a correlated pair. A specific scenario is examined where an optical cavity contains multiple two-level atoms, including one that's been intentionally entangled with another, while the remaining atoms are separate. When a laser drives the cavity and interacts with the two-level atoms, our analysis shows that the entanglement between the cavity and the single atom can result in the creation of W-state entanglement among the total group of atoms, thereby indicating that systems with partial correlations are capable of demonstrating highly quantum phenomena.

This report details the advancements made to the silicon pixel detector of the CMS detector at the LHC, which were completed in mid-2016. During the initial runs at the LHC, the original pixel detector processed close to $700\, \text{pb}^{-1}$ of data, before upgrade work was undertaken. Once finished, the pixel detector's performance significantly improved, enabling it to record and analyze nearly $360\, \text{fb}^{-1}$ of data following the LHC's record-breaking runs at high energies. To achieve these results, the analysis involves combining multiple production channels of the Higgs boson decaying into two photons within the context of the Standard Model, while accounting for various background processes, ultimately yielding a measured signal strength consistent with theoretical predictions, with a degree of accuracy.

We present volume-dependent corrections to the flat-space glueball spectrum for quantum chromodynamics, with corrections parametrized by the four-volume of the gauge theory. This parametrisation is particularly useful for understanding finite-volume lattice simulations. A leading-order finite-volume correction to the mass spectrum is derived analytically using a worldline instanton method based on the heat-kernel expansion. Furthermore, we show that the determinant of the worldline operator can be computed using zeta function regularisation in arbitrary finite volumes. A numerical determination of the higher-order correction terms to the mass spectrum is also performed.

Social media platforms offer valuable insights into public opinion and behavior, yet extracting these insights poses significant challenges. Twitter, in particular, provides a wealth of real-time information but is characterized by massive data volumes. To tackle this challenge, deep learning techniques such as LSTM have shown great promise in text classification. This study examines two approaches to improving LSTM performance in classifying the sentiment of tweets: data expansion through synthetic SMS-like transformations and transfer learning by training on a larger, related dataset. Our results indicate that both methods yield enhanced accuracy, ultimately achieving a 91.1% classification rate.

Building on previous work, our research extends the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter from Q^2 to Q^4 within the Einstein-Yang-Mills theory, affecting black hole solutions, and then incorporates those changes into a holographic model. In the resulting framework, we find that both the non-linear charge parameter and the holographic scalar field mass parameter significantly impact the "shadow radius-to-horizon radius" ratio of black holes, with the former exhibiting a non-linear relationship, and also influence the shape of black hole thermal profiles, with the former causing a shift in the peak temperature and the latter resulting in a broader distribution. Notably, our findings suggest that black holes with higher mass to entropy ratios may be associated with younger ages.

A novel approach to quantum state characterization is presented, which latches onto the intuitive visual representation offered by optical tomography. The method is rooted in the decomposition of tomographic data into cloud profiles, each corresponding to a specific phase-space trajectory and quantifiable energy. The analysis highlights the effectiveness of this approach in deciphering the nonintuitive quantum phenomena observed in Gouberakises states, specifically the evolution of entanglement and the emergence of interference patterns. The role of a specific parameter in these states is also explored through a quantitative assessment of their distribution.

The success of recent deep learning advancements in dialogue management relies heavily on the availability of large datasets. A potential obstacle to overcoming this limitation is the immense computational cost associated with training on substantial datasets. Our research demonstrates that dialogue specifications can enhance the performance of a trained model by reducing the required training data. We demonstrate this concept by presenting a model called QuDiMo, which combines a pre-trained language model with a concise set of rules to generate responses that appear natural and contextually relevant. By utilizing a small set of carefully designed prompts, QuDiMo effectively addresses the challenges of the dialogue generation process, resulting in a significant improvement in the quality of the responses produced.

A significant financial burden on agriculture is imposed by plant diseases, which can cause yield losses of up to 50%.  In addition, a lack of real-time data and the difficulty in predicting disease outbreaks make it challenging to forecast yields and pricing.  This study proposes a method for predicting the pressure of disease, yield, and market price in real-time, which can aid farmers in making informed decisions about the management of crops.  Using a case study of strawberry cultivation, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach.  Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to assess the impact of pressure of disease, price, and yield on profit, and the results showed that the model is effective in estimating the model's latent variables and their effects on profit.  Furthermore, a cost-benefit analysis of pressure management of disease was conducted, which indicated that the model has the potential to increase profit by properly managing disease pressure.

As 5G technology becomes a reality and panoramic streaming platforms like YouTube 360 and Netflix 360 gain popularity, the challenge of efficient bandwidth utilization for immersive video transmission is being addressed by predictive methods. These approaches focus on predicting the user's future viewpoint within the panoramic video to deliver a tailored, high-quality view. While various techniques aim to predict the user's viewpoint, they often rely solely on the user's historical view, neglecting valuable information present in video content. This study introduces a novel viewpoint prediction method that leverages immersive video features, including panoptic video technology and subtitles, to enhance prediction accuracy. By incorporating a subtitle interpretation network, the model utilizes information from both the user's historical view and video content to make precise accuracy predictions. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through extensive testing on multiple datasets, with promising results.

We have developed a novel projected operator product state (POPS) approach for accurately representing thermal states and time evolution of one-dimensional periodic lattice systems in thermal environments. The projections for both thermal states and time evolution are carried out using thermofield dynamics, while the description of the lattice's thermal state is achieved by introducing auxiliary duplicate sites. In this method, the projected thermal states and time-evolved states correspond to slice PEPS (pslicePEPS) with U(1) symmetry. Our analysis into the structure of peps slices reveals that these states can be described by a constant bond dimension, regardless of the PEPS slice width. Consequently, we demonstrate the computational efficiency of peps slices by providing examples of thermal phases and time-evolved states on a periodic lattice after a quench, driven by a bosonic Hamiltonian. As a result, we confirm the ability of peps slices to faithfully capture thermal phases and time-evolution dynamics on a periodic lattice.

Using Taylor-based expansion and canonical surfaces, we create a general decoupling framework for an extensive class of smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space. The bound obtained through this framework depends on the scale $\sigma$ and the surface's curvature $\kappa$ in the following way: the bound is $\sigma^{2/3}$ for regions of unit curvature and declines as $\sigma^{1/3} \Delta \kappa$ between adjacent patches of unit curvature, where $\Delta \kappa$ signifies the change in curvature across the patches.

This paper introduces a new concept of volume growth for anisotropic $W^{1,X(\Omega)}$-capacity, which leads to novel, anisotropic versions of relative isoperimetric and Lorentz-Sobolev inequalities, as well as an anisotropic variant of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality.

In measuring accelerations experienced in space, particularly microgravity, unexpected sudden shifts known as glitches can occur, potentially influencing scientific studies. These spikes in acceleration can result from various sources, such as minor propulsion system overactivations or different forces, and are often identified through visual inspections of data graphs. We developed an automated system to detect glitches using pattern recognition techniques and machine learning, which can operate independently of the raw data used in scientific analysis. Our system successfully identified known glitches from previous studies and discovered additional, unreported events, demonstrating its capability to efficiently process and flag a large number of events in a much shorter amount of time compared to visual inspections. With further development, this system has the potential to be integrated with data analysis systems to provide researchers with a comprehensive list of potential glitches for thorough examination.

We've observed how certain dimers move through a two-dimensional space, and it seems they can use a method of motion, and it can be compared to a steering wheel in a car. We've also found that this "reversal effect" in these dimers doesn't follow the usual rules of a reversal found in larger devices. A mathematical model has been developed to explain this behavior, and we've found a way to measure how this "steering" influences the movement. We've even found a connection between this effect and a change in the way the dimers move. Finally, we've discovered that this effect may have useful applications in creating machines that can move more efficiently.

This paper explores various cover problems centered on k-strong shortest path unions. We begin by establishing a significant finding, revealing that the k-strong shortest path union cover problem belongs to the NP-complete category. Following this, we address specific instances of cover problems. Notably, we prove that the k-strong shortest path cover problem is NP-complete and hard to approximate within a factor of 2 in log n. We also examine the 2-strong shortest path multicut problem, discovering it is NP-complete for unit weights. However, we also identify a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for 2-strong shortest path multicut when the number of target components needed to be merged is limited to k. We also examine another cover problem variant, the k-strong shortest path branch cover. Finding a 2-strong shortest branch cover is shown to be NP-complete and hard to approximate within a factor of 2 in log n. Nevertheless, we present an algorithm with an approximation factor of O(k log^2 k) for the k-strong branch cover problem.

A study of global fits for generalized parton distributions is ongoing, with emphasis on the Omega-shaped parameterization of the gluon distribution in protons. This parameterization exhibits singular behavior at specific values of the momentum transfer squared, which can be classified into three types based on their divergence. Using the dispersion relation technique from quantum field theory, we relate these singularities to the ambiguity in non-perturbative estimates of power corrections known as $\zeta$-evolution. Our analysis shows that for the dominant singularities, the uncertainties associated with the estimation of the gluon distribution are significantly lower than those of the sea quark distribution, as they are directly linked to the gluon matrix elements rather than the squared ones. Furthermore, quantum field theory constraints on the fit results allow us to constrain the appropriate range of the dimensionality parameter in the theory, ultimately influencing the shape of the gluon distribution curve. This methodology offers a unique way to incorporate the principles of quantum field theory into global fits, providing a framework for evaluating and comparing different parameterizations of parton distributions.

We investigate the relationship between a tree's structure and the frog model's behavior on that tree, specifically its transience or recurrence. Our research shows that for any non-deterministic frog model with initially stationary frogs, there's a degree threshold $D$ such that if the tree's maximum degree is $>D$, the model's behavior is guaranteed to be transient, while if its maximum degree is $2$, the behavior is recurrent under certain conditions. Additionally, our findings on finite exothermic frog models reveal that the degree threshold can be lowered, while in the case of the deterministic frog model, the threshold remains unchanged from its random counterpart.

We experimentally investigate the interference of surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly in a magnetophotonic crystal, causing a distinct peak in the magneto-optical spectral features. A peak position predicted by a surface plasmon wave vector is confirmed, and its stability under a varying magnetic field is observed. Additionally, we demonstrate that peak intensity can be controlled through sample thickness due to the interference between the Rayleigh anomaly and surface plasmons. This control method's potential applications include the development of compact magnetic field sensors.

We investigated a novel, decision-based approach to knowledge distillation, termed decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, which allows a secondary network to learn from an primary network it cannot directly access. Unlike traditional knowledge distillation, this method only utilizes the target network's final classification outcome, rather than its internal representations. We adapted two common DB3 models by employing an auxiliary network to process the input data and extract features, which we found to be crucial in preventing the model from being misled and replicating the target network's input-output behavior. Our experimental findings, across multiple image benchmarks, confirm that our proposed approaches significantly outperform decision-based knowledge distillation and even some white-box training methods.

The uncertainties linked to hadronic inputs account for approximately 90% of the total uncertainties regarding the QCD electroweak input. We have calculated the branching fractions and CP asymmetries for the decays $\bar{B}^0\to K^+K^-$ and $J/\psi K^+K^-$, as well as their direct CP asymmetries, while taking into account the resonant contributions from $e^+e^-\to J/\psi K_L$ decays. The uncertainties arising from hadronic inputs could also explain up to 30$\%$ of the total uncertainties in some branching fraction and CP asymmetry measurements.

Given a module $M$ within the category of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ with high multiplicity, specific properties hold for its components, making lattice reconstruction feasible. These properties also aid in recovering the module's composition factors from $M$'s lattice. However, the reconstruction process becomes complicated when a specific factor appears with multiplicity two or more, whether as a distinct component or part of a set of equivalent modules.

The Strong Geodetic Recognition Problem involves determining whether a specific vertex set in a graph is the unique fixed point of some function that selects a maximum number of distinct locations between any two adjacent vertices. This paper aims to address the problem by characterizing a class of graphs called trees for which the given vertex set is the fixed point of such a function, and also discusses implications for a broader class of graphs known as c-trees.

Imitation learning is a concept that allows robots to acquire new tasks by observing human demonstrations, but traditionally it required extensive interactions between the robot and human. In the imitative learning process, the robot must efficiently use the collected data to minimize the number of demonstrations per new task. We present a novel algorithm in imitation learning named TRAIL, which allows the robot to use past experiences to reduce the number of demonstrations needed on new tasks. By optimizing a set of policies through neural networks in imitation learning, TRAIL enables the robot to apply what it has learned from multiple tasks to new tasks with few demonstrations. We show in experiments on navigation tasks that the robot can generalize from 100 unrelated maps to 1000 new maps, achieving a significant improvement over traditional imitation learning methods.

Experts who collaborate on complex tasks can collaboratively accomplish them more efficiently than individuals who learn separately from isolated expert instructions. This observation motivates co-imitation learning, a novel framework that leverages multiple agents learning from several experts who learn together by observing and learning from one another, as well as from external expert demonstrations. The framework enables multiple learners who observe one another while collaborating on the same task, thereby providing a biologically plausible explanation for why nature has created several mirroring brain areas that allow humans to internalize expert instructions by simply watching one another. We develop an algorithm for co-imitation learning and show that it statistically outperforms existing methods that rely on expert demonstrations when applied to multiple robotic learning from collaborative human instructors in various experiments.

In the context of using a Berlekamp-Massey algorithm for efficient decoding of Reed-Solomon codes within a noisy channel, we investigate the impact of introducing a cutoff rate (or bias) into the sequential decoding process. By introducing a cutoff rate, we find that not only does it lead to a more efficient decoding with a comparable error probability, but it also results in a more accurate outcome compared to introducing a random bias. Furthermore, by applying a cutoff rate, we observe that the decision variable in the sequential decoding converges to a normal distribution as block length increases, with a scaling factor of the square root of the block length. By accounting for the impact of a finite cutoff rate, we are able to derive the corresponding probability of error, which converges to a specific value as the cutoff rate becomes extreme. Notably, by comparing the probability of error for a finite cutoff rate to that of an infinite decoder, we find that the former results in a cutoff rate that yields the minimum average computation while maintaining a fixed probability of error, which has a minimum cutoff rate value of approximately 0.5444 and corresponds to a bias value of approximately 0.324.

We investigate the potential of incorporating task information into action representations within a reinforcement learning framework to enhance task execution. This concept is demonstrated effectively in the challenge of neural machine translation, a complex parsing task. By incorporating additional task-specific information into the action representation within the reinforcement learning policy, we observe a significant improvement in translation accuracy. Notably, this method requires no changes to the original algorithm or prior knowledge of task characteristics, providing a universally applicable solution. Moreover, we explore the possibility of using task-related information within the action representation in a transfer learning context, and the results indicate a notable improvement in performance during learning and a generalization ability across different translation languages.

This research focuses on improving the robustness of end-effector pose estimation relative to the traditional method, specifically in response to inaccurate object localization and the misalignment of the target. A novel approach to 6D pose estimation is proposed, leveraging a depth camera to accurately measure the distance between the target and the camera, even when the camera's coordinate system does not align with that of the target. This additional depth information is incorporated into the 6D pose estimation algorithm, which is then utilized for optimizing task planning in a feedback loop. The proposed approach is thoroughly tested and the results demonstrate the following improvements compared to the baseline: up to a 30% reduction in 6D pose estimation error, as well as a 25% decrease in end-closer target alignment error and a 20% reduction in the distance estimation error from the depth camera.

This paper builds upon our earlier work in Ref.9, further developing the notion of QFS-spaces. We introduce the idea of continuous retracts within QFS-spaces and demonstrate their connection to idempotents in QFS-spaces. Additionally, we explore the presence of continuous retracts in spaces of names and show that continuous retracts in QFS-spaces correspond to nameless types in programming language theory.

The extent of polarization present in online forums and social media platforms is amplified by negative correlations between user engagement and the spread of political viewpoints, as well as by the hierarchical hyperlinks that organize the Web's information, which together contribute to polarization's overall magnitude.

We examine the parsing capabilities of certain Thrufy language classes, specifically focusing on determining the word problem for two particular Thompson group variants, G_{0.5} and G_{0.25}. By leveraging existing structure-theoretic properties and new insights, we establish that the word problem for the Thompson group G_{0.5} can be solved using a deterministic context-free language and a finite set of constraints related to tensor products. Additionally, a specific Thrufy subclass with a deterministic context-free word problem is identified. We prove that the word problem for the Thompson group G_{0.25} requires more complex parsing capabilities, specifically two passes over the input, and a context-free language is insufficient to solve it.

We propose a method for enabling mutual information exchange between a quantum device and its environment without any external input necessary. This is accomplished by creating an interconnected network that utilizes two types of isolators: one that transfers signals from the device to its surroundings, and another that transfers signals from the surroundings to the device. The unique design of our proposed network allows the quantum system to not only receive input from its environment but also generate an identical response when triggered by an external signal, effectively demonstrating that bidirectional signaling is equivalent to the equivalence of two triggered reactions. The feasibility of this concept has been demonstrated through practical applications, including the differentiation between two individuals based on their voice and the distinction between taste in the realm of flavor.

We've developed a modified version of the Koiso operator suitable for measuring curvature in Euclidean space, and through this, we've re-evaluated a condition for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal in Euclidean space. By combining this revised operator with specific mathematical techniques, we've established a new, more general criterion for biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space. Hypersurfaces formed by rotating certain types of curves in Euclidean space can now be identified as examples of biharmonic shapes.

We examine two primary consequences of the $a_u$MSM model that are relevant to cosmology and particle physics. Firstly, we show that the a_uMSM model resolves the issues of the stability of the electroweak vacuum and the amount of dark matter in the universe by introducing a new scale around one TeV and linking it to the Higgs sector through nonperturbative effects, potentially leaving detectable imprints on the vacuum decay and dark matter annihilation. Secondly, we argue that the a_uMSM model provides a mechanism to resolve the strong CP problem without axial U(1) anomalies, offering natural light pseudoscalars that can be classified as potential inflatons or moduli fields.

The LAMOST time-domain survey has been completed and 2.5 million time-domain spectra have been analyzed for variability. A total of 11.1 million light curves were created and through various statistical methods a total of 1.1 million variable stars and a total of 822 clusters were identified and classified. We introduce the concept of Edge-Gated CNNs, or EG-CNNs, as a novel method to incorporate object boundary information into CNNs for the purpose of precise image segmentation. By integrating an EG-Module that seamlessly combines low-resolution feature maps with edge maps through concatenation and convolutional layers, the EG-CNN enhances its processing capabilities. The EG-Module's design allows for the injection of object boundary information while maintaining a computationally efficient structure. The impact of EG-CNNs is demonstrated through various experiments on challenging image segmentation benchmarks, where the EG-CNN's superiority over conventional U-Net-based CNNs is evident in its ability to produce more accurate object delineations. The EG-Module's ability to improve the EG-CNN's performance with minimal additional computational cost is clearly shown, resulting in a 3.6% increase in DSC without any additional parameters or significant computational burden. The EG-CNN's design and effectiveness are further validated through comprehensive ablation studies and comparisons with the current state-of-the-art methods. The source code for the EG-CNNs is made available on GitHub.

This research investigates the precise isolation guarantees provided by specific MongoDB cluster configurations. By integrating formal methods, we verify that seven different scenarios of single-threaded snapshot isolation are met or exceeded, including three previously undefined situations. Our analysis indicates that certain MongoDB deployments are prone to data inconsistencies, as seen in cases like a lost update scenario with a specific query pattern. To conduct this study, we either extended the existing, publicly accessible RAMDisk format definitions or developed new ones to accurately represent the behavior of various MongoDB cluster setups, such as WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER with WiredTiger storage engine. Notably, we found that a combination of a single-threaded snapshot isolation guarantee and another isolation property can exceed the data correctness provided by certain MongoDB deployments, such as a specific write-skew scenario with a given application logic.

We establish that certain subsets of e-positive functions within the graded components of the Cooperstein homology are precisely those subsets of the homology of Dyck paths whose indices sum to a specific value. This result is achieved by demonstrating a direct relationship between the e-positivity of chromatic symmetric functions assigned to Dyck paths and their underlying area statistics, made apparent via Macdonald polynomial expansion. As a consequence, we can transfer this positivity from the Cooperstein homology to the ordinary homology, thereby enhancing an earlier finding of Escobado and Hu.

We introduce a novel trained hindsight loss function, which we believe mimics the learning process of summarizing attended information to minimize prediction errors in the face of a noisy environment. Our approach to minimizing prediction error through hindsight summarization can be effectively modeled using a trained compressor in a communication setting. Our findings demonstrate that the trained compressor successfully embodies the concept of attended prediction error minimization, particularly in scenarios involving a joint source-channel code, and outperforms the trained Compress-and-Forward algorithm in min-cut max-flow settings. Notably, we find that using an expanded code space results in a more efficient compressor that substitutes the need for a separate communication channel. Our research also highlights the potential of using a compressor to implement a hindsight loss function, and introduces the concept of attaining a more optimal policy through the efficient transmission of a compressed representation of attended information rather than a full prediction error signal.

Implicit biases present in datasets can distort models' understanding and restrict their effective application, a significant challenge in medical image analysis. While prior research has addressed bias mitigation through various techniques, the development of models that accurately reflect human perception remains a challenge. In this work, we introduce a new task, Vision Tasks Deception Detection (V2D), with the goal of identifying implicit biases in models created from eye-tracking data. A new dataset has been assembled, incorporating three models trained on diverse subsets of the public ISIC 2018 dataset. A new metric, False Deception Rate (FDR), has been defined to measure the success of models in deceiving clinicians. Through the V2D task and False Deception Rate, we aim to uncover and document explicit or subtle implicit biases in medical image learning models, a critical step towards creating reliable models that accurately reflect human perception.

We study the magnetic properties of a special type of network called the triangular Ising spin glass, which consists of Ising spins connected in clusters of three by random magnetic interactions. Although this type of network has many possible complex arrangements of interactions, our findings suggest that for two-dimensional versions, the magnetic history dependence, or "glassy" behavior, can be easily understood. By comparing our results to a simpler model that ignores the interconnected Ising spins' interactions, we observe that the history-dependent nature of the network primarily results from the specific way it's structured, not from the intricate interactions between the Ising spins themselves. Furthermore, our study shows that adding an external magnetic field and looking at how the magnetization changes over time reveal characteristic patterns, such as power laws, that provide valuable insights into the dynamics of this type of spin glass. Ultimately, our work suggests that this particular model can be a useful tool for modeling more complex, disordered materials.

A novel approach to analyzing solar energetic particle (SEP) events has been developed. This approach focuses on studying the connection between the energetic behavior of solar electrons and the characteristics of solar protons and heavy ions. It was observed that in multiple cases of large-scale SEP events seen from a 1-AU monitoring point, the behavior of solar electrons often mirrored the dynamics of solar protons and heavy ions. Conversely, at closer distances to the sun, typically less than three solar radii, the energy required to overcome the sun's gravitational pull by electrons showed significantly lower values compared to their counterparts, specifically 3.5 and 14.5 times the pull for protons and heavy ions respectively. Furthermore, a distinct asymmetrical two-component pattern with a critical threshold of around 1-10 keV was frequently seen in the distribution of this energy, a behavior that was mirrored in 81 percent of the analyzed cases, primarily during intervals when there was a substantial solar plasma flow.

This study introduces a novel application of zero-shot learning to capture the
transferability of emotions across diverse data sets. Building on this foundation,
we tackle a more intricate problem: recognizing the transferability of emotions in
natural language. To address this challenge, we devise a comprehensive framework
that employs a contrastive loss function to map textual inputs from various
corpora to a universal emotion space. This model achieves breakthrough results in
natural language emotion recognition without requiring a pre-trained corpus
specific to each target emotion. Our model excels in capturing the transferability
of emotions across different languages and corpora, yielding substantial boosts in
accuracy for both translangual and cross-corpus transfer settings. To further
validate the robustness of our approach, we experiment with multiple emotions,
corpora, and configurational parameters. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge,
this study represents a pioneering application of zero-shot learning to capture the
transferability of emotions in the domain of natural language processing.

Research on the effects of hydrostatic pressure up to 12 GPa on Bi5FeTi3O15 in its paraelectric and ferroelectric phases has been conducted, examining how 1/ \epsilon and lattice parameters respond to increasing pressure. Our results show that Bi5FeTi3O$_{15}$'s unit cell shrinks uniformly under pressure, with the unit cell volume exhibiting a 1.75 GPa inflection point. Surprisingly, the in-plane lattice parameters a and b display different behaviors under high pressure, with the volume of the (ab) plane exceeding the bulk volume at around 9 GPa. Additionally, the dielectric constant's response to pressure has been modeled, with calculations of the Landau free energy also considering the unusual lattice parameter variations under high pressure.

This paper explores the limitations of certain discrete path planning methods, such as A* and Dijkstra, in relation to optimal continuous trajectories. Our research establishes a bounded error framework for these algorithms, where the error framework is defined by specific factors including grid resolution, heuristic accuracy, state space dimensions, and distance metrics. A key benefit of this framework is its ability to predict state-specific errors, allowing for a more precise assessment of the discrepancy between approximated and optimal paths. We propose a re-search strategy to mitigate state-related errors and illustrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulation studies. The results highlight the efficiency of targeting states with high errors and the potential to evaluate the accuracy of discrete paths without computing optimal trajectories.

If we consider a classical adiabatic shock wave in an otherwise homogeneous universe, its rapid expansion creates a region where the adiabatic parameter is greater than a critical value. This critical threshold is where the shock wave generates a coherent graviton mode, effectively breaking the symmetry of the adiabatic mode. Researchers have previously shown that in scenarios with a significant excess over this threshold value, the energy dissipates, causing the pressure to decline exponentially, ultimately expelling matter from that region and creating an expanding void. In this paper, we investigate whether the coherent gravitational mode will be affected by this matter expansion or if it will be damped by the infalling surrounding matter. Our analysis reveals that the matter expansion does have a significant impact, as the matter's kinetic energy, influenced by the shock wave, overwhelms the gravitational mode inside the void, preventing the void from collapsing. As a result, we anticipate a transition to a regime of mixed modes, where the mode's amplitude will be balanced by the difference between the critical value and the adiabatic parameter value.

We compare the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubach and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks for predicting decay rates, addressing hadron interactions with a lepton and a virtual gauge boson in $e^+e^-$ scattering, $\tau$ decays, and $B$ meson decays. Although both models are based on rigorous final-state Hilbert space construction, they differ in how decay rates are expressed as matrix elements. Consequently, the factorization properties of the two approaches diverge to varying degrees, and to bypass the associated uncertainty, direct, model-independent relations to matrix elements must be applied to ensure precise predictions. These 1999 insights are relevant to current and upcoming $e^+e^-$, $\tau$, and $B$ factory operations.

A comprehensive analysis of 1D supersymmetric quantum non-singular potentials in detail is undertaken in this study. The research highlights the existence of a polynomial version of the Heisenberg algebra with degrees of three for these potentials, in contrast to linear Heisenberg algebra for the harmonic oscillator, resulting in five-fold algebraic differences. Specific examples such as the harmonic oscillator, Mie-1D, and Coulomb potentials are identified as harmonic oscillators under various coordinate transformations within the SUSY quantum framework. Additionally, the study reveals the potential for creating a new family of SUSY quantum potentials through the harmonic oscillator as the starting point, unlike traditional cases where the potential is modified through coordinate transformations. Furthermore, the polynomial quantum algebra is utilized to establish a direct relationship with the shape invariance property of these potentials.
A new formula has been created to calculate a variation-based Lyapunov exponent for systems that possess an invariant measure which is non-smooth, including chaotic systems known as Yang-Lee gases.

Measurements were conducted on asymmetric SQUID circuits consisting of one large and two small Josephson junctions. The presence of phase synchronization between the junctions leads to lower critical currents in the SQUID than in a single Josephson junction with equivalent phase coherence. Conversely, the absence of synchronization results in equivalent critical current values. These findings are supported by an appropriate Josephson physics based model.

A new approach to calculating the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, Casimir energy and pressure has been proposed based on path integral formulation. This method was used to find the corresponding thermodynamic properties of pure $ \mathrm{SU}(2) $ Yang-Mills theory in one spatial dimension, revealing the impact of the non-abelian aether term on Casimir energy and pressure in such systems. Notably, the linear size of the box affects these properties, which, in turn, can influence the phase structure of high temperature Yang-Mills systems through the one-loop thermodynamics derived from pure Yang-Mills at high temperatures in large finite volume.

This study examines the challenge of pricing liquidity-adjusted European options, which necessitates considering the expense of hedancing the position. We develop a technique to calculate expected hedancing expenses before placing a European option, under a geometric Brownian motion model with stochastic interest rates, yielding an adjusted option price. This method yields comparable results to a Monte Carlo simulation, but with significantly greater computational efficiency. For stochastic interest rate models, our technique provides results quickly, contrary to the potential complexity of Monte Carlo calculations, especially in the case of Brownian motion models with singularities, which require massive simulation runs. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to three specific models: HMM, Vasicek, and Cox-Ingersoll-Ross interest rate models.

Recent research into optimal conductivity distribution within diverse materials requires exploring complex functionals with varied coefficients, as the objective function's linear nature demands the consideration of linear differential constraints similar to the Maxwell model. To analyze such problems with significant heterogeneity, a comprehensive framework for Γ-convergence is established for functionals subject to linear differential constraints, allowing for a detailed examination of gradient regularization term reduction, periodic homogenization, and three-scale convergence, with an emphasis on ensuring stability during limit processes.

This study investigates the properties of tidal structures within early-type galaxies from the KEPLER dataset, specifically focusing on their flux fraction, projected size, and ionized oxygen content in relation to the galaxies' mass and mass distribution. Our analysis reveals the following key findings: tidal structures become less common in more massive galaxies, their electron content is significantly lower, and their mass distribution mirrors that of the main galaxy, indicating a strong correlation with the galaxies' mass. These results suggest a shift in the tidal structures' characteristics at the knees of the mass-luminosity curves, providing valuable insights into the evolution of early-type galaxies.

Distinguishing individuals based on their past performance is crucial for determining their future opportunities. However, imperfect information about past performance can lead to disparities in future opportunities, creating inequalities that perpetuate across generations. A dynamic model illustrating a repeated principal-agent relationship was developed to analyze the impact of allocation mechanisms on opportunity disparities. Two specific strategies - equal opportunity treatment and opportunity tied to performance information were modeled. The study found that unequal distribution of opportunities can create significant disparities across generations due to socioeconomic feedback effects. Notably, unexpected actions that provide equal opportunities to all agents can have a lasting impact, generating inequalities in future generations. A model incorporating a large population size was developed, and the conditions under which performance-based opportunity allocation results in inequalities across generations were analyzed. It also found that actions promoting equal opportunities can result in inequalities in multiple subsequent generations.

Complex laser systems based on nonlinear optics consist of numerous interconnected components, each with its own nonlinear properties. These properties make modeling and simulation challenging. In this study, a comprehensive NLO-based model is presented, along with a discussion on the difficulties associated with modeling individual components. As an illustration, the modeling of a particular type of soliton laser is demonstrated, showing the advantages of a rigorous numerical approach in achieving high accuracy.

The well-known fact that a linearly reduced dimension version of the unit ball in ell_2 space exists with epsilon-isometric accuracy, we show that linearily reducing dimension versions of the unit ball in ell_p space (for p not equal to 2) are impossible with epsilon-isometric accuracy for any p other than the value 2, not just for extreme values less than 1 or greater than 2. A similar result (with an exponential version) applies to linearily reducing dimension versions of the unit ball in lambda_p space for all p other than the value 2 as well. Notably, we establish that for 1 < p less than 2, linearily reducing dimension versions of the unit ball in ell_p space are not 1/n to the power of 1/(2-p)-eta isometric for any value of eta. Our results for linearily reducing dimension versions of ell_p and lambda_p spaces have analogous formulations in metric space reductions (for ell_p) or directed graph D-greedy reductions (for lambda_p).
